## Learning goals

This chapter sets out the facts of economic growth and the tools we use to study them. By the end
of it you will be able to:

- describe how recent sustained growth is, and how unevenly it spread across countries;
- define a growth rate and derive the **constant growth rule** $y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t$ by applying one year's
  growth again and again, and explain why compounding makes the yearly increase grow;
- take logs to show why a **ratio scale** draws constant growth as a straight line, and derive the exact doubling
  time and the **Rule of 70** from it;
- derive the formula for the average annual growth rate between any two years, explain why it is a geometric
  mean, and compute it from data;
- derive the rules for the growth rates of products, ratios and powers from logarithms, apply them to the
  Cobb-Douglas production function, and read their comparative statics;
- reshape, filter, combine and summarize data tables with pandas, and draw line charts, scatter plots and step
  charts with Plotly Express;
- go beyond the textbook's countries: pick any of about 170 countries and compare data from two sources.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper for the website versions with many countries (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_menu(fig, shown, regions, label="Textbook countries"):
    """Draw the countries in `shown` and put every other country one click away in the legend.

    `regions` maps each country to its region. With more than 40 countries, a menu above the plot
    chooses the region whose countries the legend lists. Traces that are not countries stay as they are.
    """
    countries = [trace.name for trace in fig.data if trace.name in regions]
    groups = [label] + sorted(set(regions[name] for name in countries))
    if len(countries) <= 40:
        groups = [None]                                 # a short legend lists every country at once
    buttons = []
    for group in groups:
        visible = []
        for trace in fig.data:
            if trace.name in shown:
                visible.append(True)
            elif trace.name not in regions:
                visible.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            elif group is None or regions[trace.name] == group:
                visible.append("legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=group, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    if len(groups) > 1:
        menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
        fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig
```

## Model overview

This chapter is about **economic growth**: the steady rise in income per person that has made people in many countries far richer than their great-grandparents. It presents facts rather than an economic model. But reading those facts takes a small toolkit: what a growth rate is, what a constant growth rate does to a number over many years, why a ratio scale turns that growth into a straight line, how long a variable takes to double, and how growth rates combine when variables are multiplied, divided or raised to a power. Every later chapter uses these tools, so this section derives each of them step by step.

There are four blocks, from the basic definition to the results built on it: growth rates and the constant growth rule; logarithms, the ratio scale and the Rule of 70; the average annual growth rate; and the rules for the growth rates of products, ratios and powers. At the end, `### The model in code` turns the tools into Python functions and checks every result with numbers. The sections after it apply the tools to data: growth over two thousand years, U.S. growth on a ratio scale, growth across countries, poverty counted by people, and the growth rules in U.S. data.

A bar over a letter marks a value we hold **constant** and take as given, such as a constant growth rate $\bar{g}$ for income or $\bar{n}$ for population. A subscript is the year: $y_t$ is the value of $y$ in year $t$, and $y_0$ its value in the starting year. A growth rate without a bar, such as $g_x$, may differ from one year to the next. In the code we simply write `g` and `n`.

<!-- cell -->

### Growth rates and the constant growth rule

#### Definitions

Let $y_t$ be any variable that we measure once a year, such as GDP per person or the population. Its **growth rate** between year $t$ and year $t+1$ is its percentage change: the change in the variable divided by its value at the start ([Appendix C.2](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.2-percentages-ratios-and-index-numbers)),

$$g_t \equiv \frac{y_{t+1} - y_t}{y_t} = \frac{\Delta y_{t+1}}{y_t}.$$

A growth rate of $0.02$ means 2 percent a year. Two features of this definition matter below. First, a growth rate has no units: GDP measured in dollars or in euros, or population counted in people or in billions, gives the same growth rate. Second, it measures change *relative to the starting level*. A country that adds \$1,000 to an income of \$10,000 grows by 10 percent; a country that adds the same \$1,000 to an income of \$50,000 grows by only 2 percent.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: one year ahead.** Suppose the growth rate takes the same value $\bar{g}$ every year. Multiply both sides of the definition by $y_t$, which gives $y_{t+1} - y_t = \bar{g}\,y_t$, and then add $y_t$ to both sides:

$$y_{t+1} = y_t + \bar{g}\,y_t = y_t\,(1+\bar{g}). \tag{1}$$

Next year's value is this year's value times the **growth factor** $1+\bar{g}$. The 1 carries over everything that is already there, and the $\bar{g}$ adds the new part, which is proportional to the current level. For a population $L_t$ that grows at the rate $\bar{n}$, equation (1) reads $L_{t+1} = L_t(1+\bar{n})$: everyone alive this year is still counted next year, and $\bar{n}L_t$ newcomers join them.

**Step 2: one year after another.** Start from $y_0$ and apply equation (1) repeatedly, each time substituting the result of the previous year:

$$y_1 = y_0(1+\bar{g}), \qquad
y_2 = y_1(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^2, \qquad
y_3 = y_2(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^2(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^3.$$

Each year contributes one more factor $(1+\bar{g})$, and a product of equal factors is a power ([Appendix C.3](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.3-exponents-and-exponential-growth)). After $t$ years there are $t$ factors:

$$y_t = y_0\,(1+\bar{g})^t. \tag{2}$$

This is the **constant growth rule**. The pattern is not a coincidence of the first three years. If equation (2) holds in some year $t$, then equation (1) gives $y_{t+1} = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t(1+\bar{g}) = y_0(1+\bar{g})^{t+1}$, so it also holds in year $t+1$, and therefore in every year.

With the starting values of Fig. 3, a population of $L_0 = 6$ billion that grows at $\bar{n} = 0.02$, equation (2) gives $L_{35} = 6 \times 1.02^{35} \approx 12.0$ billion and $L_{70} = 6 \times 1.02^{70} \approx 24.0$ billion.

**Step 3: why the yearly increase keeps getting bigger.** Equation (1) says that the increase in a year is $\Delta y_{t+1} = \bar{g}\,y_t$, a fixed percentage of a base that keeps growing. So the absolute increase is larger every year, and a chart of $y_t$ against $t$ bends upward. Compare this with **simple growth**, which adds the same amount $\bar{g}\,y_0$ every year, so that $y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g}t)$. Multiplying out the growth factor for two years shows where the two part ways:

$$(1+\bar{g})^2 = 1 + 2\bar{g} + \bar{g}^2.$$

The terms $1 + 2\bar{g}$ are simple growth. The extra $\bar{g}^2$ is growth earned in the second year on the growth of the first year. This is **compounding**, and over many years such extra terms pile up. At 2 percent for 35 years, simple growth multiplies the starting value by $1 + 35 \times 0.02 = 1.7$, while compound growth doubles it: $1.02^{35} \approx 2.0$.

*Intuition.* Under a constant growth rate, the growth itself grows. Each year's increase becomes part of the base on which next year's growth is earned.

#### What the results predict

- **Paths that bend upward.** Under constant growth the level rises by a larger amount every year. That is why the population of Fig. 3 and U.S. GDP per person in Fig. 2 both curve upward on an ordinary scale, even though their growth rates hardly change.
- **Small differences in growth rates become large differences in levels.** Take two economies that start at the same level $y_0$. Writing equation (2) for both and dividing, $y_0$ cancels: $y^A_t/y^B_t = \left[(1+\bar{g}_A)/(1+\bar{g}_B)\right]^t$. Over 100 years, growth of 1 percent a year multiplies income by $1.01^{100} \approx 2.7$, growth of 2 percent by $1.02^{100} \approx 7.2$, and growth of 3 percent by $1.03^{100} \approx 19.2$.
**Comparative statics.** Taking logs of equation (2) ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)) gives $\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\ln(1+\bar{g})$. Each coefficient is an elasticity:

| A change in ... | changes $y_t$ by ... | reason |
|---|---|---|
| the starting value $y_0$, up 1% | $+1\%$, in every year | $\ln y_0$ enters with coefficient 1 |
| the growth factor $1+\bar{g}$, up 1% | about $+t$ percent | $\ln(1+\bar{g})$ enters with coefficient $t$ |
| the growth rate $\bar{g}$, up 0.01 (one percentage point) | $\ln y_t$ rises by about $0.01\,t/(1+\bar{g})$ | the derivative of $\ln(1+\bar{g})$ is $1/(1+\bar{g})$ ([Appendix C.7](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.7-derivatives-and-marginal-thinking)) |
| the horizon $t$, longer | any gap in growth rates matters more | $t$ multiplies $\ln(1+\bar{g})$ |

Raising growth from 2 to 3 percent for 100 years raises $\ln y_t$ by about $100 \times 0.01/1.02 \approx 0.98$, which multiplies the final level by about $e^{0.98} \approx 2.7$ (exactly, $1.03^{100}/1.02^{100} \approx 2.65$). A change in the starting level shifts the whole path by the same percentage forever. A change in the growth rate has an effect that grows every year.

<!-- cell -->

### Logarithms, the ratio scale and the Rule of 70

#### Definitions

A **ratio scale** is a vertical axis whose equally spaced tick marks carry numbers with a constant ratio, such as 6, 12, 24, 48 (each twice the one before) or 1, 10, 100, 1,000 (each ten times the one before). On such an axis the height of a point is proportional to the *logarithm* of its value, not to the value itself. Moving up by one tick multiplies the value by the same factor, wherever on the axis you start. Plotly draws this kind of axis with `log_y=True` or `type="log"`.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: constant growth is a straight line in logs.** Take the natural logarithm of both sides of equation (2). The log of a product is the sum of the logs, and the log of a power is the exponent times the log ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)):

$$\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\,\ln(1+\bar{g}). \tag{3}$$

The right-hand side is a straight line in $t$, with intercept $\ln y_0$ and slope $\ln(1+\bar{g})$. For small growth rates $\ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}$ ([Appendix C.6](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.6-approximations)); for instance $\ln 1.02 = 0.0198$. Between any two years $t_1$ and $t_2$ the slope, rise over run in logs, is

$$\frac{\ln y_{t_2} - \ln y_{t_1}}{t_2 - t_1} = \ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}.$$

So on a ratio scale, constant growth draws a straight line, and the slope of that line is (very nearly) the growth rate.

**Step 2: the doubling time.** How many years does it take until $y_t = 2y_0$? Put $y_t = 2y_0$ into equation (2) and divide both sides by $y_0$. The starting level drops out:

$$2y_0 = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2 = (1+\bar{g})^t.$$

The unknown sits in the exponent, so take logs of both sides, $\ln 2 = t\,\ln(1+\bar{g})$, and divide by $\ln(1+\bar{g})$:

$$t_{\text{double}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+\bar{g})}. \tag{4}$$

**Step 3: the Rule of 70.** Equation (4) is exact, but hard to evaluate in your head. Two approximations make it easy: $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$, and $\ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}$. Write the growth rate in percent as $g = 100\,\bar{g}$, so that $\bar{g} = 0.02$ means $g = 2$. Then

$$t_{\text{double}} \approx \frac{0.693}{\bar{g}} = \frac{69.3}{g} \approx \frac{70}{g}. \tag{5}$$

Why 70 and not 69.3? The log of $1+\bar{g}$ is a little smaller than $\bar{g}$ itself, about $\bar{g} - \bar{g}^2/2$. Dividing by $\bar{g}$ instead of by $\ln(1+\bar{g})$ therefore makes the doubling time come out slightly too short, and rounding 69.3 up to 70 makes up for it at growth rates of a few percent. (It also divides evenly by 1, 2, 5, 7 and 10.) At 2 percent the exact answer is 35.0 years, $69.3/2$ gives 34.7 and $70/2$ gives 35.

The same steps give the time to grow by any factor $m$: $t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})$. And after $k$ doubling times a variable is $2^k$ times its starting value. At 2 percent, 70 years are two doubling times, so the variable grows by a factor of $2^2 = 4$: the 6 billion people of Fig. 3 become 24 billion after 70 years.

*Intuition.* Logs turn multiplying into adding. Constant growth multiplies by the same factor every year, so in logs it adds the same amount every year, and that is a straight line.

#### What the results predict

- **The doubling time depends only on the growth rate.** The starting level cancelled in step 2. A poor country and a rich country that grow at the same rate double their incomes in the same number of years.
- **Faster growth shortens the doubling time in proportion.** By the Rule of 70 the doubling time is inversely proportional to the growth rate, an elasticity of $-1$. Doubling the growth rate halves the doubling time; growth that is 10 percent faster, 2.2 instead of 2.0 percent a year, shortens it by about 9 percent, from 35 to about 32 years.
**How to read a ratio-scale chart.**

| On a ratio scale you see ... | it means ... | because ... |
|---|---|---|
| a straight line | constant growth | equation (3) is linear in $t$ |
| a steeper straight line | faster growth | the slope is $\ln(1+\bar{g}) \approx \bar{g}$ |
| a line that bends upward (flattens) | growth that speeds up (slows down) | the slope changes |
| two parallel lines | equal growth rates and a constant ratio of levels | the vertical gap is $\ln y^A - \ln y^B = \ln(y^A/y^B)$ |
| equal vertical steps | equal *percentage* changes | each tick is the same ratio |

<!-- cell -->

### The average annual growth rate

#### Definitions

Real data rarely grow at a constant rate. Suppose we know a variable's value $y_0$ in a starting year and $y_t$ in a year $t$ years later. Its **average annual growth rate** $\bar{g}$ is the constant growth rate that would take it from $y_0$ to $y_t$ in exactly $t$ years.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: turn the constant growth rule around.** In equation (2) we knew $y_0$ and $\bar{g}$ and computed $y_t$. Now $y_0$, $y_t$ and $t$ are known and $\bar{g}$ is the unknown. Divide both sides of equation (2) by $y_0$:

$$\frac{y_t}{y_0} = (1+\bar{g})^t.$$

**Step 2: undo the power.** Raise both sides to the power $1/t$. Since $\left((1+\bar{g})^t\right)^{1/t} = (1+\bar{g})^{t/t} = 1+\bar{g}$ ([Appendix C.3](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.3-exponents-and-exponential-growth)), we get $(y_t/y_0)^{1/t} = 1+\bar{g}$.

**Step 3: subtract 1** from both sides:

$$\bar{g} = \left(\frac{y_t}{y_0}\right)^{1/t} - 1. \tag{6}$$

This is the **rule for computing growth rates**. For $t = 1$ it gives $y_1/y_0 - 1 = (y_1 - y_0)/y_0$, the definition of a growth rate we started from. Applied to the population path of Fig. 3, which goes from 6 billion to $6 \times 1.02^{100} \approx 43.5$ billion in 100 years, it gives back $\bar{g} = 7.245^{1/100} - 1 = 0.02$.

**Step 4: the same rule in logs.** Take logs of the equation in step 1 and divide by $t$:

$$\ln(1+\bar{g}) = \frac{\ln y_t - \ln y_0}{t}.$$

The right-hand side is the slope, on a ratio scale, of the straight line that joins the first and the last point. The dashed line in Fig. 5 uses the same idea, but fits all the years at once.

**Step 5: an average of growth factors.** If the yearly growth rates $g_1, g_2, \dots, g_t$ differ, applying equation (1) once for each year gives

$$y_t = y_0\,(1+g_1)(1+g_2)\cdots(1+g_t).$$

Compare this with equation (2): $(1+\bar{g})^t$ must equal the product of the yearly growth factors. So $1+\bar{g}$ is their **geometric mean**, not the plain average of the growth rates. Here is why the difference matters. A variable that rises by 10 percent and then falls by 10 percent has a plain average growth rate of zero, yet it ends lower, because $1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99$. Equation (6) gets this right: $0.99^{1/2} - 1 \approx -0.5$ percent a year.

*Intuition.* The average annual growth rate is the one steady pace that starts and ends at the same two points as the data.

#### What the results predict

- **Only the end points matter.** Equation (6) uses $y_0$, $y_t$ and $t$ and nothing in between. Booms and slumps inside the period count only through the level at which they leave the variable at the end.
**Comparative statics.** From the log version, $\ln(1+\bar{g}) = (\ln y_t - \ln y_0)/t$:

| A change in ... | changes $\ln(1+\bar{g})$, close to $\bar{g}$, by ... |
|---|---|
| the final value $y_t$, up 1% | about $+0.01/t$ |
| the starting value $y_0$, up 1% | about $-0.01/t$ |
| the length $t$, longer, with the same ratio $y_t/y_0$ | less: the same total growth is spread over more years |

**Long-run growth rates are robust.** Over 100 years, a 1 percent error in the final level moves the average growth rate by only about 0.01 percentage points. Over a single year, the same error moves it by a full percentage point. That is one reason why the growth rates of Fig. 5 and Fig. 7 are more reliable than any single year's number.

<!-- cell -->

### Growth rates of products, ratios and powers

#### Definitions

Suppose two variables $x$ and $y$ grow at the rates $g_x$ and $g_y$. We want the growth rate $g_z$ of a variable $z$ built from them. One fact does all the work: the change in the log of a variable is approximately its growth rate. From the definition, $v_{t+1}/v_t = 1+g_v$ for any variable $v$, so

$$\Delta\ln v_{t+1} \equiv \ln v_{t+1} - \ln v_t = \ln\frac{v_{t+1}}{v_t} = \ln(1+g_v) \approx g_v.$$

#### Deriving the results

**The product rule.** Let $z_t = x_t \times y_t$. Taking logs gives $\ln z_t = \ln x_t + \ln y_t$. This holds in every year, so we can write it for year $t+1$ and for year $t$ and subtract the second from the first: $\Delta\ln z = \Delta\ln x + \Delta\ln y$. Replacing each change in logs by the growth rate it approximates ([Appendix C.5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.5-growth-rates-and-the-growth-rules)):

$$z = x \times y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_z = g_x + g_y. \tag{7}$$

**The ratio rule.** Let $z_t = x_t/y_t$. Now $\ln z_t = \ln x_t - \ln y_t$, and the same subtraction gives

$$z = \frac{x}{y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_z = g_x - g_y. \tag{8}$$

**The power rule.** Let $z_t = x_t^a$ for any number $a$: positive, negative or a fraction. Now $\ln z_t = a\ln x_t$, so $\Delta\ln z = a\,\Delta\ln x$ and

$$z = x^a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g_z = a \times g_x. \tag{9}$$

For a whole-number power you can also see it from the product rule: $x^2 = x \times x$ grows at $g_x + g_x = 2g_x$. Each rule replaces an operation by a simpler one, which is exactly what logs do: multiplying becomes adding, dividing becomes subtracting, and a power becomes a multiple.

**How exact are the rules?** With yearly data the product rule holds exactly for growth *factors*: $1+g_z = (1+g_x)(1+g_y)$, so $g_z = g_x + g_y + g_x g_y$. The leftover term is the product of two small numbers; at 2 and 1 percent it is $0.02 \times 0.01 = 0.0002$. The same is true of the ratio rule, $1+g_z = (1+g_x)/(1+g_y)$, and of the power rule, $1+g_z = (1+g_x)^a$. The rules hold exactly for growth rates measured as changes in logs, or in continuous time.

**Combining the rules.** Joining (7) and (9), a variable $z = x^a y^b$ grows at $g_z = a\,g_x + b\,g_y$. The most important case in this book is the Cobb-Douglas production function of Chapter 4, $Y_t = A_t K_t^{1/3} L_t^{2/3}$. The product rule (7), used twice for the three factors, gives $g_Y = g_A + g_{K^{1/3}} + g_{L^{2/3}}$. The power rule (9) turns the last two terms into multiples:

$$g_Y = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}\,g_K + \tfrac{2}{3}\,g_L. \tag{10}$$

Output per person is $y = Y/L$, so the ratio rule (8) subtracts $g_L$:

$$g_y = g_Y - g_L = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}g_K + \tfrac{2}{3}g_L - g_L = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}\left(g_K - g_L\right) = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}\,g_k,$$

where the last step uses the ratio rule once more for capital per person, $k = K/L$.

*Intuition.* Output grows as fast as productivity, plus the growth of each input weighted by its exponent. Per person, only productivity growth and the growth of capital per person are left, and capital per person counts only one third. Chapters 4 to 6 build on this decomposition.

#### What the results predict

- **Equal growth rates keep a ratio constant.** If $g_x = g_y$, the ratio rule gives $g_{x/y} = 0$. On a ratio scale, two countries growing at the same rate draw parallel lines, as the United States and the United Kingdom do after 1950 in Fig. 6.
- **GDP, population and GDP per person.** Total GDP is GDP per person times the population, $Y = y \times L$, so $g_Y = g_y + g_L$, or equivalently $g_y = g_Y - g_L$. In the U.S. data of Fig. 9, GDP per person grew about 1.9 percent a year since 1870 and the population about 1.4 percent, so total GDP grew about 3.3 percent. Fast GDP growth with equally fast population growth leaves income per person where it was.
**Comparative statics of equation (10)**, with each growth rate raised by one percentage point while the others stay the same:

| One point faster growth of ... | raises $g_Y$ by | raises $g_y$ by |
|---|---|---|
| productivity $A$ | 1 point | 1 point |
| capital $K$ | 1/3 point | 1/3 point |
| labor $L$ | 2/3 point | $-1/3$ point (the same capital is spread over more workers) |
| capital and labor together | 1 point | 0 (constant returns to scale) |

<!-- cell -->

### The model in code

We now turn the tools into Python functions. Each function's description names the equation it computes. The cells after it check every result above with numbers.

> **Python note.** `def` creates a *function*: a named recipe that takes inputs (the
> *arguments*) and gives back a result with `return`. The text in triple quotes is a short
> description of what the function does. `**` means "to the power of", and `np.log` is the natural logarithm.

```{python}
def constant_growth(y0, g, t):
    """Value after t years of constant growth at rate g: y_t = y0 (1 + g)^t   (equation 2)."""
    return y0 * (1 + g) ** t


def growth_rate(y0, yt, t):
    """Average annual growth rate between two values t years apart: (yt / y0)^(1/t) - 1   (equation 6)."""
    return (yt / y0) ** (1 / t) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes to double at growth rate g: ln 2 / ln(1 + g)   (equation 4)."""
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)
```

**Check 1: compounding.** We follow the population of Fig. 3, 6 billion people growing at 2 percent, and
compare compound growth, equation (2), with simple growth, which adds the same 2 percent of the *starting*
value every year.

> **Python note.** A `for` loop repeats its indented lines once for each value in the list after `in`, here
> the years 1, 35, 70 and 100. An *f-string* such as `f"{x:.2f}"` inserts the value of a variable into a piece
> of text: `:.2f` shows two decimals, and `:8.2f` also pads the number to 8 characters so the columns line up.

```{python}
print("Years   compound growth, eq. (2)   simple growth")
for t in (1, 35, 70, 100):
    compound = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, t)
    simple = 6.0 * (1 + 0.02 * t)
    print(f"{t:5d}   {compound:15.2f} billion   {simple:8.2f} billion")
```

After 35 years compound growth has doubled the population, and after 70 years quadrupled it. Simple growth
gets only to 1.7 and 2.4 times the start.

**Check 2: a straight line in logs.** Equation (3) says that the log of a constantly growing variable rises
by the same amount, $\ln(1+\bar{g})$, every year.

> **Python note.** `np.arange(0, 6)` gives the whole numbers 0, 1, ..., 5, and `constant_growth` then works on
> all of them at once. `np.log` takes the log of every value, `np.diff` subtracts each value from the next one,
> and `.round(4)` keeps four decimals.

```{python}
years = np.arange(0, 6)
L = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, years)
print("Population (billions):    ", L.round(4))
print("Yearly change in ln L:    ", np.diff(np.log(L)).round(5))
print(f"Slope of eq. (3), ln(1.02): {np.log(1.02):.5f}   (close to g = 0.02)")
```

**Check 3: the Rule of 70.** We compare the exact doubling time, equation (4), with the approximations of
equation (5), and confirm that the population really is twice as large after one exact doubling time.

```{python}
print("Growth rate   exact, eq. (4)   69.3 / g   Rule of 70, eq. (5)")
for g in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.07):
    G = 100 * g                                     # the growth rate in percent
    print(f"{G:9.0f}%   {doubling_time(g):14.2f}   {69.3 / G:8.2f}   {70 / G:19.2f}")
print(f"At 2%, after {doubling_time(0.02):.2f} years: {constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, doubling_time(0.02)):.3f} billion")
```

The Rule of 70 is within half a year of the exact answer at these growth rates. In relative terms its error
grows once growth rates go well beyond a few percent: at 7 percent it is off by more than 2 percent.

**Check 4: the average annual growth rate.** Equation (6) must undo equation (2), the log version of step 4 must
agree with it, and the geometric mean of step 5 must give the right answer where the plain average does not.

```{python}
end = constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, 100)
print(f"6 billion at 2% for 100 years:          {end:.2f} billion")
print(f"Equation (6) gives back:                {growth_rate(6.0, end, 100):.4f}")
print(f"Log version, exp(slope) - 1:            {np.exp((np.log(end) - np.log(6.0)) / 100) - 1:.4f}")
print(f"One year, t = 1 (a percentage change):  {growth_rate(6.0, 6.3, 1):.4f}")
print(f"Up 10% then down 10%, two years:        {growth_rate(1.0, 1.10 * 0.90, 2):+.4f}   (not 0)")
higher = growth_rate(6.0, 1.01 * end, 100)
print(f"Final value 1% higher: the growth rate rises by {100 * (higher - 0.02):.4f} percentage points")
```

**Check 5: the growth rules.** We take the U.S. growth rates of Fig. 9, 1.9 percent for GDP per person and
1.4 percent for the population, and compare each rule with the exact growth over one year.

```{python}
gy, gL = 0.019, 0.014                               # GDP per person and population, U.S. since 1870 (Fig. 9)
y0, L0 = 1.0, 1.0
y1, L1 = y0 * (1 + gy), L0 * (1 + gL)               # the values one year later
print(f"Product  y x L:    rule (7) {gy + gL:.5f}   exact {(y1 * L1) / (y0 * L0) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Ratio    y / L:    rule (8) {gy - gL:.5f}   exact {(y1 / L1) / (y0 / L0) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Power    y^(1/3):  rule (9) {gy / 3:.5f}   exact {y1 ** (1 / 3) / y0 ** (1 / 3) - 1:.5f}")
print(f"Power    L^(-2):   rule (9) {-2 * gL:.5f}   exact {L1 ** -2 / L0 ** -2 - 1:.5f}")
change_logs = np.log(y1 * L1) - np.log(y0 * L0)
print(f"In logs the product rule is exact: {change_logs:.5f} = {np.log(1 + gy) + np.log(1 + gL):.5f}")
```

Each rule misses the exact answer by less than a tenth of a percentage point (the cross term, here
$0.019 \times 0.014 \approx 0.0003$ for the product), and in logs the product rule holds exactly. The **Your turn** after Fig. 9 checks equation (10) in the same way.

## Growth over the very long run

Sustained growth is a recent event in human history. We start with two thousand years of income data and then zoom in on the United States.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 1: Economic growth over the very long run

**Goal.** See how recent sustained growth is.

The figure shows GDP per person over the last 2,000 years for six countries, measured as a multiple of
500 dollars (2011 prices), which is roughly the level at which people can barely survive. Later in this
section you can add any of the 169 countries of the Maddison Project.

```{python}
longrun = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-1.csv")
longrun.tail()
```

The table is **wide**: one column per country. Plotly Express prefers **long** tables, with one row per
country and year.

> **Python note.** `.melt(id_vars="year")` turns the country columns into rows: the old column names go
> into a new column (`var_name`) and the numbers into another (`value_name`). `.map(NAMES)` then replaces
> each column name with a readable country name, using the dictionary `NAMES`. `.dropna()` removes the
> few years without an estimate, so that the lines join their neighbors.

```{python}
NAMES = {"gdppc_x500_usa": "United States", "gdppc_x500_jpn": "Japan", "gdppc_x500_gbr": "United Kingdom",
         "gdppc_x500_arg": "Argentina", "gdppc_x500_chn": "China", "gdppc_x500_gha": "Ghana"}
longrun = longrun.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="series", value_name="gdp").dropna()
longrun["country"] = longrun.series.map(NAMES)
longrun.head()
```

The textbook shows six countries, but the Maddison Project estimates GDP per person for 169. We load
a second file with every country at the same benchmark years, and keep the countries that are not
already in `longrun`. For the six textbook countries we keep `longrun`, which also uses Maddison's older
estimates for the earliest years (the textbook's data).

> **Python note.** `~` means "not", so `~table.country.isin(names)` keeps the rows whose country is *not*
> in `names`. `pd.concat([a, b])` stacks two tables on top of each other; columns that exist in only one of
> them are filled with `NaN` (missing). `.rename(columns={old: new})` renames a column so the two tables match.

```{python}
world_longrun = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_longrun.csv")
others = world_longrun[~world_longrun.country.isin(longrun.country)]
everyone = pd.concat([longrun, others.rename(columns={"gdppc_x500": "gdp"})])
print(everyone.country.nunique(), "countries")
others[others.year == 1].head()
```

Very few countries have an estimate for the year 1: for most of them the data begin in 1820, 1870 or
1950. A line that starts late means *no data*, not *no income*.

Each country keeps one color in every chart of this notebook, so a country is easy to follow when you
add others. On the website, a menu shows the textbook's countries together with one region at a time, so the
countries of each region need colors that differ from each other. The function `group_colors` hands them out.

```{python}
LIGHT = {"#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"}      # too pale on white
PALETTE = []                                                                   # 44 colors
for c in px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if c not in LIGHT and c != "#2E91E5":
        PALETTE.append(c)
PALETTE.append("#2E91E5")                       # too close to the book's U.S. blue: used last
```

> **Python note.** `group_colors` gives the countries their colors one at a time. For each country, the list
> `used` collects the colors already given to the countries shown together with it, and the country takes the
> first palette color that is not in `used`, preferring one that no country has yet. If every color is taken, it
> takes the one that `used` counts least often (`.count`), searching from the end of the palette (`reversed`).
> `dict(fixed or {})` starts from a copy of the fixed colors (or an empty dictionary), and `continue` skips to
> the next country.

```{python}
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """Give each country a color that no other country in its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    groups: the lists of countries shown together (menu views); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                       # the colors of the countries shown with `name`
        for group in groups:
            for other in group:
                if name in group and other in colors:
                    used.append(colors[other])
        free, unused = [], []
        for c in PALETTE:
            if c not in used:
                free.append(c)
                if c not in colors.values():
                    unused.append(c)                    # no country has this color yet: the best choice
        least = PALETTE[-1]
        for c in reversed(PALETTE):                     # no free color: the one used least, from the end
            if used.count(c) < used.count(least):
                least = c
        colors[name] = (unused + free + [least])[0]
    return colors
```

The eight countries of the textbook's figures get fixed colors of our palette. Each group lists the countries
that one region view shows together: the eight, plus the countries of that region.

> **Python note.** `.groupby("country").region.first()` gives each country's region, taken from its first row.
> `region_of[region_of == region].index` lists the countries of one region.

```{python}
BOOK_SIX = ["United States", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "Argentina", "China", "Ghana"]
FIRST = BOOK_SIX + ["South Africa", "India"]                  # the countries of the textbook's figures
BOOK_COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "Japan": TEAL, "United Kingdom": GREEN, "Argentina": "#5aa0d8",
               "China": "#0b4f47", "Ghana": "#e0a33b", "South Africa": "#b04a5a", "India": "#6c5b9e"}
region_of = world_longrun.groupby("country").region.first()
REGION_GROUPS = []                                            # one group per region view
for region in sorted(region_of.unique()):
    REGION_GROUPS.append(FIRST + list(region_of[region_of == region].index))
COLORS = group_colors(sorted(region_of.index), REGION_GROUPS, BOOK_COLORS)
```

The title of the chart reports how many times GDP per person grew in one of the chosen countries: the
United Kingdom when it is chosen, otherwise the first country in your list. The function `short` turns a long
official name into the usual short one, so that titles stay on one line.

> **Python note.** `px.line` draws one line per value of `color=`; `markers=True` adds a dot for each
> estimate, and `log_y=True` gives a ratio scale (Fig. 4 explains it). `color_discrete_map=COLORS` gives each
> country its own color. `interact` calls the function and draws the figure again every time you change a
> control: a `Dropdown` is a menu of choices, `ToggleButtons` is a row of buttons, and a `SelectMultiple` is a
> list from which you pick several countries by holding Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) while clicking. The `;` at the end
> only hides an extra line of text. In `short`, `name.split(" (")[0]` cuts the text at " (" and keeps the
> first piece, and `SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)` looks the name up in the dictionary, returning it unchanged
> when it is not there. `a if condition else b` gives `a` when the condition is true and `b` otherwise.

```{python}
SHORT_NAMES = {"Republic of Korea": "South Korea", "D.R. of the Congo": "DR Congo", "Russian Federation": "Russia",
               "Taiwan, Province of China": "Taiwan", "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong", "U.R. of Tanzania": "Tanzania",
               "Lao People's DR": "Laos", "Republic of Moldova": "Moldova", "Syrian Arab Republic": "Syria"}


def short(name):
    """A short country name for titles, e.g. 'Bolivia (Plurinational State of)' -> 'Bolivia'."""
    name = name.split(" (")[0].split(":")[0]                      # drop '(...)' and ': Mainland'
    return SHORT_NAMES.get(name, name)


def very_long_run(start=1, scale="linear", countries=tuple(BOOK_SIX)):
    """Fig. 3.1: GDP per person (multiples of $500) from the year `start` to 2022."""
    chosen = everyone[(everyone.year >= start) & everyone.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdp", color="country", markers=True, log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdp": "GDP per person (multiple of 500 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    if chosen.empty:
        fig.update_layout(title=f"No data for the chosen countries since the year {start}")
        return fig
    name = "United Kingdom" if "United Kingdom" in set(chosen.country) else chosen.country.iloc[0]
    one = chosen[chosen.country == name]
    factor = one.gdp.iloc[-1] / one.gdp.iloc[0]
    label = "U.K." if name == "United Kingdom" else short(name)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{label} GDP per person in {one.year.iloc[-1]} was {factor:.0f} times "
                            f"its level in the year {one.year.iloc[0]}")
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500])
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(very_long_run,
         start=Dropdown(options=[1, 1500, 1700, 1820, 1900, 1950], value=1, description="first year", style=WIDE),
         scale=ToggleButtons(options=["linear", "ratio"], description="vertical scale"),
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(set(everyone.country)), value=tuple(BOOK_SIX), rows=8,
                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with every country (region menu and legend), scale buttons and a range slider
fig = very_long_run(countries=tuple(BOOK_SIX) + tuple(sorted(set(others.country))))
fig.update_layout(title=very_long_run().layout.title.text)       # the title of the textbook view
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0.01, y=0.98, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", buttons=[
    dict(label="linear scale", method="relayout", args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True,
                                                         "yaxis.tickvals": None}]),
    dict(label="ratio scale", method="relayout", args=[{"yaxis.type": "log", "yaxis.autorange": True,
                                                        "yaxis.tickvals": [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500]}])])])
country_menu(fig, BOOK_SIX, world_longrun.groupby("country").region.first())
```

(Bolt and van Zanden 2024, [doi:10.34894/INZBF2](https://doi.org/10.34894/INZBF2));
for the earliest years of the textbook's six countries, Angus Maddison's own estimates, the
[Maddison Database 2010](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-database-2010).
Prepared files: [`data/ch03/fig3-1.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/fig3-1.csv) and [`data/ch03/maddison_longrun.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/maddison_longrun.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

*On the website: choose a region in the menu above the chart, then click a country in the legend to add it.*

**What to notice.**

- For almost all of history, GDP per person stayed between 1 and 3 times the subsistence level, in every
  country (only the United Kingdom had pulled a little higher by 1500–1700). Then, in the last two or three
  centuries, it shot up: the curve looks like a hockey stick.
- Growth started at different times: first in the United Kingdom and the United States, later in Japan and
  Argentina, and only in the last few decades in China. Ghana's rise is much smaller.
- Choose a first year of 1820 or 1900 to stretch out the modern era, and switch to the ratio scale to
  separate the lines.
- Add Italy and Egypt, two of the few countries with an estimate for the year 1. Italy, the center of the
  Roman Empire, was then richer than any of the textbook's six countries, and Egypt was about as rich as China. Today
  Italy has about 62 percent of U.S. GDP per person and Egypt about 23 percent.

#### Key numbers: the Great Divergence

```{python}
latest = longrun[longrun.year == 2022].set_index("country").gdp
print((latest / latest["United States"]).round(2))
```

In 2022, Japan and the United Kingdom had about 2/3 of U.S. GDP per person, Argentina and China about
1/3, and Ghana about 1/14. Before 1700, incomes across countries probably differed by a factor of 2 or 3
at most. This widening of the gaps is called **the Great Divergence**.

### Fig. 2: Per capita GDP in the United States

**Goal.** Look at modern growth in one country, year by year, then compare countries.

We load two files. `fig3-2.csv` holds the official U.S. series of the textbook figure: the national
accounts of the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) from 1929 to 2025, joined to Maddison's estimates before
1929. `maddison_world.csv` holds the Maddison Project's GDP per person and population for every country and
every available year from 1870 to 2022, in the same 2022 dollars.

```{python}
us = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-2.csv")
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
world.tail()
```

The function draws the U.S. alone from the official series, as the textbook does. As soon as you add a
country, every line, the U.S. one included, comes from the Maddison Project, so that all countries are
measured in the same way. The title then compares the richest and the poorest country you chose.

> **Python note.** `tuple(countries) == ("United States",)` checks whether the U.S. is the only country
> chosen. `.assign(country="United States")` adds a column with the same value in every row.
> `.groupby("country").last()` keeps the last row of each country, here its latest year, and `.idxmax()`
> gives the label of the largest value.

```{python}
def income_chart(countries=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 3.2: GDP per person (2022 dollars); the U.S. alone uses the official series to 2025."""
    if tuple(countries) == ("United States",):
        chosen = us.assign(country="United States")
    else:
        chosen = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", color_discrete_map=COLORS,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    latest = chosen.groupby("country").last()
    if chosen.empty:
        fig.update_layout(title="Choose at least one country")
    elif len(latest) == 1:
        first, last = chosen.iloc[0], chosen.iloc[-1]
        label = "U.S." if first.country == "United States" else short(first.country)
        fig.update_layout(title=f"{label} GDP per person grew about {last.gdppc / first.gdppc:.0f}-fold "
                                f"from {first.year} to {last.year}")
    else:
        rich, poor = latest.gdppc.idxmax(), latest.gdppc.idxmin()
        fig.update_layout(title=f"{latest.year.max()}: GDP per person {latest.gdppc.max() / latest.gdppc.min():.0f} "
                                f"times higher in {short(rich)} than in {short(poor)}")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(income_chart,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value=("United States",), rows=8,
                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
official = income_chart().data[0]
official.name = "United States, official data"
fig.add_trace(official)
fig.update_layout(title=income_chart().layout.title.text)          # the title of the textbook view
country_menu(fig, [], world.groupby("country").region.first())
```

**Sources.** Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis via FRED: [real GDP (`GDPCA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPCA), [population (`B230RC0A052NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/B230RC0A052NBEA)
and [GDP deflator (`A191RD3A086NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A191RD3A086NBEA), from 1929;
before 1929 and for every other country: [Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per capita (`gdppc`) and population, Groningen Growth and Development Centre](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)
(Bolt and van Zanden 2024, [doi:10.34894/INZBF2](https://doi.org/10.34894/INZBF2))
(the textbook uses the Barro-Ursúa data before 1929).
Prepared files: [`data/ch03/fig3-2.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/fig3-2.csv) and [`data/ch03/maddison_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/maddison_world.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.2 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

*On the website: the official U.S. series is drawn. Choose a region in the menu, then click a country in the
legend to add it; "United States" in the legend is the Maddison estimate.*

**What to notice.**

- The curve gets steeper over time: each year, income rises by a larger *amount* than the year before.
- The *percentage* change, however, stays roughly the same, around 2 percent a year. The change in income is
  roughly proportional to its level, $y_{t+1} - y_t \approx \bar{g}\,y_t$. That is exactly what a constant growth rate means.
- Add Japan and South Korea. Korea's GDP per person was still below 2,000 dollars in 1960, and it passed
  Japan's in 2019. Gaps in the early data are real: many countries have estimates only every ten years or so before 1950.
- **Two sources, two levels.** Add any country, and the U.S. line switches to the Maddison estimate. In
  1870 it is about 6,200 dollars, a third more than the 4,634 dollars of the official series; by 2022 the two
  are within 3 percent. Both convert to 2022 dollars, but with different price indices: compare growth
  *within* a source, and levels across countries only within one source.

> **Python note.** `us.set_index("year")` uses the years as row labels, so that `gdp[1870]` gives the value
> for 1870.

```{python}
gdp = us.set_index("year").gdppc
print(f"1870: ${gdp[1870]:,}   2022: ${gdp[2022]:,}   ratio: {gdp[2022] / gdp[1870]:.1f}")
print(f"1970: ${gdp[1970]:,}   2000: ${gdp[2000]:,}   ratio: {gdp[2000] / gdp[1970]:.1f}")
```

GDP per person rose almost 17-fold between 1870 and 2022. Our 1870 value is about 10 percent higher than
the textbook's \$4,200, because we use the newer Maddison Project estimates for the years before 1929. In
the 30 years from 1970 to 2000, income almost doubled.

## The mathematics of growth

Constant growth produces a curve that bends upward, which is hard to read. These figures show why, and how a ratio scale turns that curve into a straight line.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 3: Population over time

**Goal.** See what constant growth looks like when we plot it.

Suppose the world population starts at $L_0 = 6$ billion and grows at a constant rate $\bar{n} = 2\%$ a year.
Each year the population is multiplied by $(1+\bar{n})$:

$$L_{t+1} = L_t\,(1+\bar{n})$$

This is equation (1) written for the population. Applying it year after year gives $L_t = L_0(1+\bar{n})^t$ (equation 2). The cell below checks this with a
loop: it multiplies by $1.02$ one hundred times and compares the result with the formula.

> **Python note.** A `for` loop repeats the indented lines once for each value. `range(100)` gives the
> numbers 0, 1, …, 99, so the loop runs exactly 100 times.

```{python}
L = 6.0
for year in range(100):
    L = L * (1 + 0.02)                     # equation (1), applied once per year
print(f"Year by year:  L_100 = {L:.2f} billion")
print(f"Formula (2):   L_100 = {constant_growth(6.0, 0.02, 100):.2f} billion")
```

> **Python note.** `np.arange(0, 101)` gives the whole numbers 0, 1, …, 100. `go.Figure()` starts an empty
> chart, and `add_trace` adds a curve to it. In the widget cell, a `FloatSlider` chooses a number between `min`
> and `max` in steps of `step`; `readout_format=".3f"` shows it with three decimals.
> `L[-1]` is the last value of the array, and `max(100, 1.05 * L[-1])` is the larger of the two numbers: the
> vertical axis stays at 0 to 100 unless the curve would leave it.

```{python}
def population_path(L0=6.0, n=0.02):
    """Fig. 3.3: population L_t = L0 (1 + n)^t over 100 years."""
    t = np.arange(0, 101)
    L = constant_growth(L0, n, t)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Population", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"L0 = {L0:.0f} billion growing at {100 * n:.1f}% a year: after 100 years, L = {L[-1]:.1f} billion",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Year", range=[0, 102], tickvals=[20, 40, 60, 80, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Population L (billions)", range=[0, max(100, 1.05 * L[-1])]))
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(population_path,
         L0=FloatSlider(value=6, min=1, max=10, step=1, description="starting population L0", style=WIDE),
         n=FloatSlider(value=0.02, min=0.0, max=0.04, step=0.005, description="growth rate n", style=WIDE,
                       readout_format=".3f"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 3 with a precomputed slider for the growth rate
# Growth rates above 2.5% would leave the start figure's vertical axis (0 to 100), which the website keeps fixed
slider_figure(population_path, "n", [0.0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015, 0.02, 0.025], start=0.02, label="growth rate n")
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 3.3 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- At 2 percent a year, 6 billion people become 43.5 billion after a century, more than seven times as many.
  (This is only an illustration: demographers expect population growth to fall toward zero.)
- The curve bends upward, just like U.S. GDP per person in Fig. 2. A constant growth rate adds a larger
  amount each year, because it applies to a larger base.
- From this picture alone, it is hard to tell whether the growth rate is constant. Fig. 4 fixes that.

### Fig. 4: Population over time, revisited

**Goal.** Learn to read a **ratio scale**, on which constant growth is a straight line.

At 2 percent a year, the population doubles about every 35 years (Rule of 70: $70/2 = 35$). It goes from 6 to
12, 24 and 48 billion. On a **ratio scale**, the vertical axis is labeled 6, 12, 24, 48: each step doubles
the one before. Equal distances then mean equal *percentage* changes, so a constant growth rate draws a
straight line.

> **Python note.** `make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, ...)` makes a figure with two panels side by side, and
> `row=1, col=2` sends a trace to the second one. `np.arange(0, 106, T)` gives 0, T, 2T, … up to 105. On a
> ratio-scale axis, the `range` is given in powers of ten: `np.log10(150)`.

```{python}
def population_two_scales(n=0.02):
    """Fig. 3.4: the same population path on (a) a standard scale and (b) a ratio scale."""
    T = doubling_time(n)
    t = np.linspace(0, 105, 200)
    dots = np.arange(0, 106, T)                                   # every doubling time
    L, L_dots = constant_growth(6, n, t), constant_growth(6, n, dots)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) Standard scale: the curve bends upward", "(b) Ratio scale: a straight line"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Standard scale", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Ratio scale", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4)), row=1, col=2)
    for col in [1, 2]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=dots, y=L_dots, name="Each doubling", mode="markers", showlegend=(col == 1),
                                 marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Year", range=[-3, 108], tickvals=[25, 50, 75, 100])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Population L (billions)", range=[0, 85], row=1, col=1)      # fixed: room for n = 2.5%
    fig.update_yaxes(type="log", range=[np.log10(4.5), np.log10(150)], tickvals=[6, 12, 24, 48, 96], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"n = {100 * n:.1f}%: doubles every {T:.1f} years (Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(population_two_scales,
         n=FloatSlider(value=0.02, min=0.01, max=0.025, step=0.005, description="growth rate n", style=WIDE,
                       readout_format=".3f"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 4 with a precomputed slider for the growth rate
slider_figure(population_two_scales, "n", [0.01, 0.015, 0.02, 0.025], start=0.02, label="growth rate n")
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 3.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- In panel (a), the dots are equally spaced in time (one every 35 years), but the jumps between them get
  bigger. In panel (b), the dots are equally spaced in both directions, and the curve is a straight line.
- A faster growth rate makes the line in panel (b) steeper. On a ratio scale, **the slope is the growth rate**.
- The Rule of 70 is very close to the exact doubling time for growth rates of a few percent.

### Fig. 5: U.S. per capita GDP on a ratio scale

**Goal.** Use the ratio scale to read the growth rate of real data.

Here are the data of Fig. 2 again, now on a ratio scale, with a dashed line that grows at a constant rate.
The line's level is chosen to fit the data as closely as possible (by least squares, in logarithms). You can
also choose another country; its data then come from the Maddison Project, and the vertical axis adapts.

> **Python note.** `np.log(gdp)` takes the logarithm of every value at once, and `.mean()` averages
> them. On a ratio scale, a constant growth line is a straight line in logarithms, which is why we fit it there.

> **Python note.** For a country other than the U.S., the vertical range runs from a little below the lowest
> value to a little above the highest one, in powers of ten (`np.log10`), because the axis is a ratio scale.
> `DOUBLINGS` lists tick values that double each time.

```{python}
DOUBLINGS = [250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000, 256000]


def ratio_scale_chart(g=0.02, country="United States"):
    """Fig. 3.5: GDP per person on a ratio scale, with a constant-growth line at rate g."""
    data = us if country == "United States" else world[world.country == country]
    years = data.year - data.year.iloc[0]
    level = (np.log(data.gdppc) - years * np.log(1 + g)).mean()   # best-fitting starting level
    line = np.exp(level) * (1 + g) ** years
    label = "U.S." if country == "United States" else short(country)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="gdppc", log_y=True,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), name=f"{label} data", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=data.year, y=line, name=f"Constant growth at {100 * g:.2f}%",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    low, high = 2500, 140000                                      # the textbook's U.S. range
    if country != "United States":
        low, high = min(data.gdppc.min(), line.min()) / 1.3, max(data.gdppc.max(), line.max()) * 1.3
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=DOUBLINGS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{label}: dashed line at {100 * g:.2f}% a year, doubling every "
                            f"{doubling_time(g):.0f} years")
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(ratio_scale_chart,
         g=FloatSlider(value=0.02, min=0.01, max=0.025, step=0.0025, description="growth rate of the line g",
                       style=WIDE, readout_format=".4f"),
         country=Dropdown(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value="United States", description="country",
                          style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
slider_figure(ratio_scale_chart, "g", [0.01, 0.015, 0.0175, 0.02, 0.0225, 0.025], start=0.02,
              label="growth rate of the line g")
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 5 for other countries, each with a dashed line at its own average growth rate
FIG5 = ["United States", "United Kingdom", "Japan", "Republic of Korea", "China", "India", "Brazil",
        "Argentina", "Botswana", "Ghana", "D.R. of the Congo", "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)"]

    figures.append(ratio_scale_chart(round(g, 4), name))
fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[0].layout)
```

(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/README.md)).

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- The data stay close to a straight line with a slope of about 2 percent a year for more than 150 years.
  This is one of the most remarkable facts in macroeconomics.
- Look closely: before 1929 the data rise a little more slowly than the line, and from 1950 to 2005 a
  little faster. The Great Depression (early 1930s) and World War II (early 1940s) are the big wiggles.
- Move the slider away from 2 percent: the line can no longer follow the data at both ends.
- Choose another country. Few follow a straight line as closely as the United States. South Korea's line is
  steep from the 1960s on, Argentina's flattens after 1975, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo's
  falls for decades. On the website, the second chart draws each country with a line at its own average
  growth rate.

## Growth across countries

Now we compare countries: their growth paths since 1870, and the link between how rich a country was and how fast it grew afterward.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 6: Per capita GDP since 1870

**Goal.** Compare the growth paths of several countries on a ratio scale.

The textbook plots one value per decade, to smooth out short-run ups and downs. We also have every
available year, from a wider data file, so you can see what the smoothing hides. We add India, which
the textbook discusses but does not draw, and you can add any other country of the Maddison Project
(the `world` table of Fig. 2).

```{python}
decades = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-6.csv").melt(id_vars="year", var_name="series", value_name="gdppc")
decades["country"] = decades.series.map({"gdppc_usa": "United States", "gdppc_gbr": "United Kingdom",
                                         "gdppc_jpn": "Japan", "gdppc_arg": "Argentina", "gdppc_zaf": "South Africa",
                                         "gdppc_chn": "China", "gdppc_ind": "India"})
annual = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_panel.csv")
levels = decades.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
japan = levels["Japan"] / levels["United States"]          # Japan relative to the U.S., by year
annual.tail()
```

The title compares one country with the United States: Japan when it is chosen, otherwise the first
country in your list. The helper `versus_us` finds the first and the last year in which both have data.

> **Python note.** `category_orders` fixes the order of the countries in the legend. `.pivot(...)` turns the
> long table into a wide one, with one row per year and one column per country. `.dropna()` then keeps the
> years in which both countries have data. `list(countries)` makes a list we can change, and `.remove(...)`
> deletes one entry from it. The vertical axis widens (once, to a fixed wider range) when a chosen country
> lies outside the textbook's range.

```{python}
def versus_us(name):
    """First and last year in which `name` and the U.S. both have data, and name's GDP per person relative to the U.S."""
    pair = world[world.country.isin([name, "United States"])].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
    ratio = (pair[name] / pair["United States"]).dropna()
    return ratio.index[0], ratio.iloc[0], ratio.index[-1], ratio.iloc[-1]


versus_us("Japan")
```

```{python}
SEVEN = ["United States", "United Kingdom", "Japan", "Argentina", "South Africa", "China", "India"]
BENCHMARKS = sorted(decades.year.unique())                     # the textbook's years: 1870, 1890, ..., 2022


def countries_since_1870(frequency="every decade", countries=tuple(SEVEN)):
    """Fig. 3.6: GDP per person on a ratio scale (2022 dollars), by decade or every year."""
    chosen = world[world.country.isin(countries)]
    if frequency == "every decade":
        chosen = chosen[chosen.year.isin(BENCHMARKS)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", log_y=True, color_discrete_map=COLORS,
                  category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)", "country": "Country"})
    others = list(countries)
    if "United States" in others:
        others.remove("United States")                            # compare the others with the U.S.
    title = "Choose a country to compare with the United States"
    if others:
        name = "Japan" if "Japan" in others else others[0]
        first, share_first, last, share_last = versus_us(name)
        title = f"{short(name)} went from {share_first:.0%} of U.S. GDP per person in {first} to {share_last:.0%} in {last}"
    low, high = 700, 90000                                        # the textbook's range ...
    if not chosen.empty and (chosen.gdppc.min() < low or chosen.gdppc.max() > high):
        low, high = 250, 300000                                   # ... or one fixed wider range
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=DOUBLINGS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_layout(title=title)
    return fig
```

```{python}
         frequency=ToggleButtons(options=["every decade", "every year"], description="data"),
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value=tuple(SEVEN), rows=8,
                                  description="countries", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
fig.update_layout(title=countries_since_1870().layout.title.text)  # the title of the textbook view
fig.update_yaxes(range=[np.log10(250), np.log10(300000)])
country_menu(fig, SEVEN, world.groupby("country").region.first())
```

(Bolt and van Zanden 2024, [doi:10.34894/INZBF2](https://doi.org/10.34894/INZBF2)), converted to 2022 dollars with the
[U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis GDP deflator (`A191RD3A086NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A191RD3A086NBEA), via FRED.
Prepared files: [`data/ch03/fig3-6.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/fig3-6.csv) and [`data/ch03/maddison_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/maddison_world.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.6 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

*On the website: choose a region in the menu above the chart, then click a country in the legend to add it.
The annual data are in the Colab version.*

**What to notice.**

- The United Kingdom was the richest country in 1870, but grew more slowly than the United States and fell
  behind it between 1890 and 1900. Since 1950 the two lines are roughly parallel: they grow at about the same rate.
- Japan grew very fast after World War II and caught up with the United Kingdom. This catch-up is called
  **convergence**.
- Argentina grew well until about 1980 and slowly since. China and India took off only in the last decades.
- Click a country in the legend to hide it; double-click to show it alone.
- Add Germany and South Korea. Germany's two world wars show up as deep dips in the annual data. Korea went
  from 7 percent of U.S. GDP per person in 1950 to 71 percent in 2022, even faster catch-up than Japan's.

#### Key numbers: growth spurts and relative incomes

> **Python note.** `.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")` turns the long table back into
> a wide one, with one column per country, so that `wide.loc[1990, "Japan"]` picks a single number.

```{python}
wide = annual.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
print(f"Japan, 1950-1990: {growth_rate(wide.loc[1950, 'Japan'], wide.loc[1990, 'Japan'], 40):.1%} a year")
print(f"China, 1978-2022: {growth_rate(wide.loc[1978, 'China'], wide.loc[2022, 'China'], 44):.1%} a year")
print(f"India, 1990-2019: {growth_rate(wide.loc[1990, 'India'], wide.loc[2019, 'India'], 29):.1%} a year")
print("Relative to the United States in 2019:")
print((wide.loc[2019] / wide.loc[2019, "United States"]).round(2))
```

Japan grew by almost 6 percent a year from 1950 to 1990, as the textbook says. In these data China grew by
about 5.6 percent a year after 1978 and India by about 4.4 percent after 1990, a bit less than the textbook
reports: the Maddison Project has revised its estimates for both countries. In 2019, China had about 30
percent of U.S. GDP per person and India about 13 percent. On a ratio scale, a gap that *looks* small can be
large: check the numbers on the vertical axis.

### Fig. 7: Levels and growth rates of per capita GDP

**Goal.** Look at growth in more than 100 countries at once.

We load a wider Penn World Table file with GDP per person and population for every country and year, and
keep the 111 countries with data since 1960, the textbook's sample.

```{python}
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_income.csv")
sample = pwt[pwt.in_sample]
sample[sample.year == 2023].sort_values("gdp_pc").head()
```

Look at the first row. Venezuela's GDP per person in 2023 appears to be about 0.1 percent of the U.S. level,
which is impossible. During Venezuela's hyperinflation the price data behind this number broke down. **Always look
at your data before using it.** We drop Venezuela and continue with 110 countries.

```{python}
sample = sample[sample.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)"]
```

Now we compute, for each country, its average annual growth rate from a starting year to 2023, and its
GDP per person in 2023 relative to the United States.

> **Python note.** `merge` joins two tables on a common column, like matching rows by ID in a
> spreadsheet. Each pass of the loop adds one table to the list `tables`, and `pd.concat(tables)` stacks
> them into one long table. `.map(SHORT)` looks each country up in the dictionary `SHORT`; countries that
> are not in it get `NaN`, which `.fillna("")` replaces with an empty text. That way only a few names are
> printed on the chart, and `POSITION` puts some of them beside their dot so that labels do not overlap.

```{python}
SHORT = {"United States": "United States", "China": "China", "India": "India", "Republic of Korea": "South Korea",
         "Botswana": "Botswana", "Singapore": "Singapore", "Japan": "Japan", "Brazil": "Brazil",
         "D.R. of the Congo": "DR Congo", "Burundi": "Burundi", "Ethiopia": "Ethiopia"}
POSITION = {"United States": "bottom right", "India": "top left", "Botswana": "bottom right",
            "Singapore": "middle left", "Japan": "bottom left", "D.R. of the Congo": "bottom center"}
end = sample[sample.year == 2023][["iso3", "country", "gdp_pc"]]
end["level_2023"] = end.gdp_pc / end[end.country == "United States"].gdp_pc.iloc[0]
tables = []
for start in [1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010]:
    first = sample[sample.year == start][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]
    table = end.merge(first, on="iso3", suffixes=("_2023", "_start"))
    table["growth"] = 100 * growth_rate(table.gdp_pc_start, table.gdp_pc_2023, 2023 - start)
    table["start_year"] = start
    tables.append(table)
growth = pd.concat(tables)
growth["label"] = growth.country.map(SHORT).fillna("")
growth["position"] = growth.country.map(POSITION).fillna("top center")
growth.head()
```

> **Python note.** `animation_frame="start_year"` adds a play button and a slider that step through the
> starting years. `log_x=True` puts the horizontal axis on a ratio scale, and `ticktext` writes the tick
> values as fractions. Each country gets its own label position, taken from the first frame (1960).

```{python}
FRACTIONS = [1 / 128, 1 / 64, 1 / 32, 1 / 16, 1 / 8, 1 / 4, 1 / 2, 1, 2]
FRACTION_NAMES = ["1/128", "1/64", "1/32", "1/16", "1/8", "1/4", "1/2", "1", "2"]
fig = px.scatter(growth, x="level_2023", y="growth", text="label", hover_name="country",
                 animation_frame="start_year", log_x=True, range_x=[1 / 100, 2.2], range_y=[-4, 9],
                 color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN],                # the color must be set here to last in every frame
                 labels={"level_2023": "Per capita GDP in 2023 (ratio scale, U.S. = 1)",
                         "growth": "Average annual growth to 2023 (percent)", "start_year": "Starting year"},
                 title=f"Average growth to 2023 ranges from {growth.growth.min():.0f} to "
                       f"{growth.growth.max():+.0f} percent a year across countries")
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=9), textfont_size=10, textposition=growth[growth.start_year == 1960].position)
fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=FRACTIONS, ticktext=FRACTION_NAMES)
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Penn World Table 11.0, real GDP at chained PPPs (`rgdpe`) and population (`pop`), Groningen Growth and Development Centre](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/)
(Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, [doi:10.34894/FABVLR](https://doi.org/10.34894/FABVLR)).
Prepared files: [`data/ch03/pwt_income.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/pwt_income.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.7 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1960 to 2023, growth rates range from about −1 to +6 percent a year. South Korea, China, Singapore,
  Botswana and Taiwan grew fastest; the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Central African Republic,
  Madagascar and Niger got poorer.
- Most countries lie between 1 and 3 percent. The cloud tilts upward, but partly by construction: the
  horizontal axis shows income *today*, and fast growth is what made a country rich today.
- Press play: for starting years 2000 and 2010 the tilt disappears, and many poor countries grew as fast as
  rich ones or faster.

```{python}
print(f"Singapore grew {g_sgp:.1%} a year: it doubles every {doubling_time(g_sgp):.0f} years")
print(f"Over 63 years its income rose by a factor of {(1 + g_sgp) ** 63:.0f}")
```

## Counting people, not countries

Weighting each country by its population changes the picture. This figure shows how many of the world's people live at each level of income.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 8: The world's population by per capita GDP

**Goal.** Count people instead of countries.

In Fig. 7 China and Luxembourg each count as one dot. Here every person counts equally. For a given year,
we sort countries from poorest to richest and add up their populations. The chart shows the percentage of
the world's population that lives in countries with GDP per person at or below each level. Income is
measured relative to the U.S. level **in 2019** for every year, so that the curves can be compared.

> **Python note.** `.cumsum()` gives running totals: the first value, then the sum of the first two, and so
> on. Dividing by the total and multiplying by 100 turns them into cumulative percentages. `.copy()` makes a
> separate table, so that adding a column does not touch `sample`. `line_shape="hv"` draws the line as steps,
> one for each country, and `add_vline` draws the dashed vertical line.

```{python}
def cumulative_shares(year):
    """Countries sorted from poorest to richest in `year`, with the cumulative share of world population."""
    table = sample[sample.year == year].sort_values("y_rel_us_2019").copy()
    table["share"] = 100 * table.pop_millions.cumsum() / table.pop_millions.sum()
    return table


def population_distribution(year=2019):
    """Fig. 3.8: cumulative share of world population by GDP per person (U.S. 2019 = 1), year vs 1960."""
    both = pd.concat([cumulative_shares(1960), cumulative_shares(year)])
    below = cumulative_shares(year)
    poor = below[below.y_rel_us_2019 < 0.05].pop_millions.sum() / below.pop_millions.sum()
    fig = px.line(both, x="y_rel_us_2019", y="share", color="year", line_shape="hv", hover_name="country",
                  log_x=True, range_x=[1 / 200, 2], range_y=[0, 102], color_discrete_sequence=[GREEN, BLUE],
                  labels={"y_rel_us_2019": "Per capita GDP (U.S. = 1 in 2019, ratio scale)",
                          "share": "Share of world population (percent)", "year": "Year"})
    fig.add_vline(x=0.05, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=FRACTIONS, ticktext=FRACTION_NAMES)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{year}: {poor:.0%} of people live below 5% of the 2019 U.S. level (dashed line)")
    return fig
```

## Rules for growth rates

Last, three handy rules: the growth rate of a product is a sum, of a ratio a difference, and of a power a multiple. We check them with U.S. data.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 9: U.S. population, GDP and per capita GDP

**Goal.** See the rules for growth rates at work.

Three rules make growth rates easy to work with (equations 7 to 9). If $x$ grows at rate $g_x$ and $y$ at rate $g_y$, then

- the product $z = x \times y$ grows at $g_x + g_y$;
- the ratio $z = x / y$ grows at $g_x - g_y$;
- the power $z = x^a$ grows at $a \times g_x$.

Total GDP is GDP per person times population, so its growth rate is the *sum* of the two growth rates. To
see this, the chart divides each series by its value in the first year, so all three lines start at 1.
For the United States we use the official series of the textbook figure. For any other country we
compute total GDP from the Maddison Project's GDP per person and population.

> **Python note.** `start, end = period` unpacks a pair of years into two variables. Dividing the table
> `table.loc[start:end]` by its first row divides every column by its own first value. An `IntRangeSlider`
> has two handles, so it chooses a whole period at once. `country_table` builds, for any country, a table
> with the same columns as `usa`. `.astype(float)` turns whole numbers with gaps into ordinary numbers.

```{python}
usa = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-9.csv").set_index("year")


def country_table(country):
    """Population (thousands), GDP per person and total GDP (billions of 2022 dollars) by year, as in `usa`."""
    if country == "United States":
        return usa                                                # the official series of the textbook
    one = world[world.country == country].set_index("year")
    table = pd.DataFrame({"population_thousands": one.pop_thousands.astype(float), "gdppc": one.gdppc})
    table["gdp_billions"] = table.gdppc * table.population_thousands / 1e6
    return table.dropna()
```

If the period starts before a country's data do, the chart starts in the country's first year, and the
title says which years it uses.

```{python}
def growth_rules_chart(period=(1870, 2025), country="United States"):
    """Fig. 3.9: total GDP, GDP per person and population, each relative to its first-year value."""
    table = country_table(country)
    start, end = period
    if end == start:                                              # both handles on one year: use one year
        end = min(start + 1, 2025)
        start = end - 1
    chosen = table.loc[start:end]
    if len(chosen) < 2:                                           # no data in the period
        return go.Figure().update_layout(title=f"No data for {short(country)} in {start}–{end}")
    start, end = chosen.index[0], chosen.index[-1]
    rates = (100 * growth_rate(chosen.iloc[0], chosen.iloc[-1], end - start)).round(2) + 0.0   # + 0.0: no "-0.00"
    chosen = (chosen / chosen.iloc[0]).reset_index().rename(columns={
        "gdp_billions": "Total GDP", "gdppc": "Per capita GDP", "population_thousands": "Population"})
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y=["Total GDP", "Per capita GDP", "Population"], log_y=True,
                  color_discrete_sequence=["#e0a33b", GREEN, BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Relative to the first year (ratio scale)", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[start - (end - start) / 20, end])   # a little room: no label in the bottom-left corner
    label = "" if country == "United States" else f"{short(country)}, "
    sign = "+" if rates.population_thousands >= 0 else "−"
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{label}{start}–{end}: GDP {rates.gdp_billions:.2f}% ≈ per capita {rates.gdppc:.2f}%"
                            f" {sign} population {abs(rates.population_thousands):.2f}% a year")
    return fig
```

```{python}
         period=IntRangeSlider(value=(1870, 2025), min=1870, max=2025, step=1, description="period", style=WIDE),
         country=Dropdown(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value="United States", description="country",
                          style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
    step.args = [step.args[0], {**step.args[1], "xaxis.range": [start - (end - start) / 20, end]}]
```
