and [GDP deflator (`A191RD3A086NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A191RD3A086NBEA), from 1929;
before 1929 and for every other country: [Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per capita (`gdppc`) and population, Groningen Growth and Development Centre](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)
(Bolt and van Zanden 2024, [doi:10.34894/INZBF2](https://doi.org/10.34894/INZBF2))
(the textbook uses Angus Maddison's earlier historical statistics).
Prepared files: [`data/ch03/fig3-9.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/fig3-9.csv) and [`data/ch03/maddison_world.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/maddison_world.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch03/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.9 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1870 to 2025, total GDP grew 3.3 percent a year, per capita GDP 1.9 percent and population 1.4
  percent. The first number is (almost exactly) the sum of the other two.
- The sum is not exact because growth over a whole year compounds: $(1+g_Y) = (1+g_y)(1+g_L)$. For small rates
  the extra term $g_y \times g_L$ is tiny.
- Population growth has slowed to less than 1 percent a year since 1980, so growth in GDP per person now
  accounts for a larger part of GDP growth. Choose a later starting year to see it.
- Choose Niger: from 1950 to 2022 its GDP grew 2.9 percent a year, but its population grew 2.8 percent, so
  GDP per person barely changed. Fast GDP growth can hide stagnant living standards. Choose Japan and a period
  that starts in 2010: its population has been shrinking since then.

#### Table 3.1: examples of growth-rate calculations

Suppose $x$ grows at 10 percent and $y$ at 3 percent a year. The rules give the growth rate of each
combination. The last column checks the rule by computing the actual one-year growth of $z$ with numbers.

```{python}
gx, gy = 0.10, 0.03
x0, y0 = 1.0, 1.0
x1, y1 = x0 * (1 + gx), y0 * (1 + gy)                          # the values one year later
rows = [
    ["z = x × y", gx + gy, (x1 * y1) / (x0 * y0) - 1],
    ["z = x / y", gx - gy, (x1 / y1) / (x0 / y0) - 1],
    ["z = y / x", gy - gx, (y1 / x1) / (y0 / x0) - 1],
    ["z = x²", 2 * gx, x1 ** 2 / x0 ** 2 - 1],
    ["z = y^(1/2)", 0.5 * gy, y1 ** 0.5 / y0 ** 0.5 - 1],
    ["z = x^(1/2) y^(-1/4)", 0.5 * gx - 0.25 * gy, (x1 ** 0.5 * y1 ** -0.25) - 1],
]
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Case", "Rule", "Exact one-year growth"]).round(4)
```

The rules are approximations, but very good ones when growth rates are small. (They hold exactly for
growth measured continuously, in logarithms.)

## Concluding remarks

- Sustained growth in living standards is very recent. It began about 200 years ago and spread unevenly, which
  produced the **Great Divergence** in incomes across countries.
- A **growth rate** is a percentage change. Growing at a constant rate, a variable is multiplied by $1+\bar{g}$ each
  year, equation (1), so after $t$ years it equals $y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t$, the constant growth rule, equation (2).
  Compounding makes the yearly increase grow, and small differences in growth rates become large gaps in levels.
- In logs, constant growth is a straight line, equation (3), so on a **ratio scale** the slope is the growth rate. A
  variable doubles in exactly $\ln 2/\ln(1+\bar{g})$ years, equation (4), or in about $70/g$ years, the **Rule of 70**,
  equation (5). U.S. GDP per person has grown at close to 2 percent a year for more than 150 years.
- The average annual growth rate between two years, equation (6), is the one constant rate that links the two end
  points: a geometric mean of the yearly growth factors.
- Growth rates differ a lot across countries, and small differences compound into huge income gaps. Counting people
  rather than countries, poverty has fallen dramatically, mainly because of growth in China and India.
- Growth rates of products are sums, of ratios are differences, and of powers are multiples, equations (7) to (9).
  Applied to the production function, they split output growth into productivity growth plus weighted input
  growth, equation (10).
- The next chapter builds a first model to explain why some countries are so much richer than others.

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): China's plan to double its economy.** China's 13th Five-Year Plan (2016–2020) set out to
"ensure that China's 2010 GDP and per capita personal income double by 2020". Its table of targets has GDP
rising from 67.7 trillion yuan in 2015 to more than 92.7 trillion yuan in 2020
([13th Five-Year Plan, official English translation, Chapter 3 and Box 2](https://en.ndrc.gov.cn/policies/202105/P020210527785800103339.pdf)).

(a) What average annual growth rate does doubling GDP in the ten years from 2010 to 2020 require?

(b) What average annual growth rate do the plan's GDP numbers for 2015 and 2020 imply? If the goal was to be
met, what does that say about growth from 2010 to 2015?

(c) The goal also named income *per person*. In this chapter's Maddison data, China's population grew about
0.5 percent a year from 2010 to 2020. How fast must total GDP grow for GDP per person to double in ten years?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Doubling means $y_t/y_0 = 2$ with $t = 10$ in equation (6). In (b), the two five-year periods must together
multiply GDP by 2. In (c), GDP per person is GDP divided by the population, so the ratio rule, equation (8), applies.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Put $y_{2020}/y_{2010} = 2$ and $t = 10$ into equation (6):

$$\bar{g} = 2^{1/10} - 1 = 1.0718 - 1 = 0.0718.$$

Doubling in ten years takes growth of about **7.2 percent a year**. The Rule of 70, equation (5), agrees: at
7.2 percent a variable doubles in about $70/7.2 \approx 9.7$ years.

**(b)** Equation (6) with $t = 5$:

$$\bar{g} = \left(\frac{92.7}{67.7}\right)^{1/5} - 1 = 1.3693^{1/5} - 1 = 0.0649,$$

about **6.5 percent a year**, the "more than 6.5 percent" of the plan's table. That is slower than the 7.2 percent
of (a), so the first five years had to be faster. Call $g_1$ the growth rate of 2010–2015. The two periods
together must double GDP. Taking the fifth root of both sides of that condition, and then dividing by 1.0649:

$$(1+g_1)^5 \times 1.0649^5 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1+g_1) \times 1.0649 = 2^{1/5}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1+g_1 = \frac{1.1487}{1.0649} = 1.0787.$$

The plan's 6.5 percent was enough only if GDP had grown about **7.9 percent a year** from 2010 to 2015.

**(c)** GDP per person is $y = Y/L$, so the ratio rule, equation (8), gives $g_y = g_Y - g_L$, or $g_Y = g_y + g_L$.
With $g_y = 7.18$ percent from (a) and $g_L = 0.5$ percent:

$$g_Y \approx 7.18 + 0.5 = 7.68 \text{ percent}, \qquad \text{or exactly} \quad (1.0718)(1.005) - 1 = 0.0772.$$

Total GDP must grow about **7.7 percent a year**: over ten years it must rise by a factor of
$2 \times 1.005^{10} = 2.10$, not 2. A goal for income per person is harder to reach than the same goal for GDP
whenever the population grows.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Greece's slump, or why a fall needs a bigger rise.** Greece's debt crisis led to
a joint rescue by the European Union and the IMF in May 2010
([IMF press release, 9 May 2010](https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2015/09/14/01/49/pr10187)). In this
chapter's data (`maddison_world.csv`, from the
[Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)),
Greek GDP per person peaked in 2008 and then fell every year until 2013:

| Year | 2008 | 2013 | 2022 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GDP per person (2022 dollars) | 37,296 | 28,816 | 32,621 |

(a) By what percentage did GDP per person fall from 2008 to 2013? By what percentage must it rise from its
2013 level to get back to the 2008 level? Show that after a fall by a fraction $x$, the rise needed is $x/(1-x)$.

(b) Use equation (6) to compute the average annual growth rate from 2008 to 2013, and from 2013 to 2022.

(c) If Greece kept growing at its 2013–2022 rate after 2022, in what year would GDP per person be back at its
2008 level? How many years of that growth did the slump of 2008–2013 undo?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(a) Write the 2013 level as $(1-x)$ times the 2008 level, and ask which factor takes it back. (c) The Model
overview shows that a variable growing at the rate $\bar{g}$ takes $t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})$ years to grow by a
factor $m$.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The ratio of the two levels is $28{,}816/37{,}296 = 0.7726$, so GDP per person fell by
$1 - 0.7726 = 0.2274$, about **22.7 percent**. To get back, it must be multiplied by $37{,}296/28{,}816 = 1.2943$:
a rise of **29.4 percent**. In general, if $y_{2013} = (1-x)\,y_{2008}$, the factor back is $1/(1-x)$, and the rise is

$$\frac{1}{1-x} - 1 = \frac{1 - (1-x)}{1-x} = \frac{x}{1-x} = \frac{0.2274}{0.7726} = 0.294.$$

The rise is larger than the fall because it starts from a lower base.

**(b)** From 2008 to 2013, $0.7726^{1/5} - 1 = -0.0503$: GDP per person fell about **5.0 percent a year**. From 2013
to 2022, $(32{,}621/28{,}816)^{1/9} - 1 = 1.1320^{1/9} - 1 = 0.0139$, about **1.4 percent a year**.

**(c)** In 2022 Greece was still $1 - 32{,}621/37{,}296 = 12.5$ percent below its 2008 level. The factor still to go
is $m = 37{,}296/32{,}621 = 1.1433$, so

$$t = \frac{\ln 1.1433}{\ln 1.0139} = \frac{0.1339}{0.0138} = 9.7 \text{ years}.$$

At 1.4 percent a year, Greece gets back to its 2008 level around **2032**, 24 years after the peak. The slump undid
$\ln 1.2943/\ln 1.0139 = 18.7$ years of growth at that rate. Over 2008–2022 as a whole, equation (6) gives
$(32{,}621/37{,}296)^{1/14} - 1 = -0.95$ percent a year. A deep slump costs living standards for a long time,
because the recovery has to climb back from a lower base.

</details>

**Problem 3 (Challenge): How long until India catches up?** The World Bank estimates that India's real GDP
must grow 7.8 percent a year on average for 22 years to reach the country's goal of high-income status by 2047;
from 2000 to 2024, growth averaged 6.3 percent
([World Bank press release, 28 February 2025](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/02/28/india-accelerated-reforms-needed-to-speed-up-growth-and-achieve-high-income-status-by-2047)).

(a) Suppose India's population grows 1.05 percent a year, its rate from 2012 to 2022 in this chapter's Maddison
data. What growth rate of GDP per person does GDP growth of 7.8 percent give? By what factor do GDP and GDP per
person rise in 22 years?

(b) A poorer country P starts with the fraction $r_0 = y^P_0/y^R_0$ of the income per person of a richer country
R. P grows at the constant rate $\bar{g}_P$ and R at $\bar{g}_R$, with $\bar{g}_P > \bar{g}_R$. Derive the number of
years $t$ until P reaches the fraction $r^*$ of R's income. Then show that the income gap halves about every
$70/(g_P - g_R)$ years, with the growth rates in percent.

(c) In the Maddison data, India's GDP per person was 13.28 percent of the U.S. level in 2022, and U.S. GDP per
person grew 1.11 percent a year from 2000 to 2022. If the U.S. kept that pace, how many years would India need to
reach half the U.S. level with the growth rate of (a)? And with its own 2000–2022 rate of 4.83 percent? (Half the
U.S. level is our yardstick, not the World Bank's definition of high income.)

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(b) Write equation (2) for both countries and divide the first by the second, so the starting levels become the
ratio $r_0$. Then take logs, as in the derivation of the doubling time, equation (4), and use $\ln(1+g) \approx g$.
(c) Start from $r_0 = 0.1328$ and aim for $r^* = 0.5$.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The ratio rule, equation (8), gives $g_y \approx 7.8 - 1.05 = 6.75$ percent, or exactly
$1.078/1.0105 - 1 = 0.0668$, about **6.7 percent a year**. In 22 years GDP rises by a factor of $1.078^{22} = 5.22$
and GDP per person by $1.0668^{22} = 4.15$.

**(b)** Equation (2) for each country gives $y^P_t = y^P_0(1+\bar{g}_P)^t$ and $y^R_t = y^R_0(1+\bar{g}_R)^t$.
Dividing the first by the second:

$$\frac{y^P_t}{y^R_t} = r_0\left(\frac{1+\bar{g}_P}{1+\bar{g}_R}\right)^t.$$

Set the left-hand side equal to $r^*$, divide both sides by $r_0$, and take logs:

$$\ln\frac{r^*}{r_0} = t\left[\ln(1+\bar{g}_P) - \ln(1+\bar{g}_R)\right]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t = \frac{\ln(r^*/r_0)}{\ln(1+\bar{g}_P) - \ln(1+\bar{g}_R)} \approx \frac{\ln(r^*/r_0)}{\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R}.$$

This is the ratio rule at work: relative income $y^P/y^R$ grows at about $\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R$, so it behaves like any
variable growing at that rate. Halving the gap means doubling the ratio, $r^*/r_0 = 2$, so
$t \approx \ln 2/(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R) \approx 0.70/(\bar{g}_P - \bar{g}_R) = 70/(g_P - g_R)$ with the rates in percent.
If $\bar{g}_P \le \bar{g}_R$, the gap never closes.

**(c)** The ratio must rise by the factor $r^*/r_0 = 0.5/0.1328 = 3.77$, and $\ln 3.77 = 1.33$.

```python
r0 = 0.1328                                    # India relative to the U.S. in 2022 (Maddison)
for g_india in [1.078 / 1.0105 - 1, 0.0483]:
    years = np.log(0.5 / r0) / (np.log(1 + g_india) - np.log(1 + 0.0111))
    print(f"India growing {100 * g_india:.2f}% a year: half the U.S. level after {years:.1f} years, around {2022 + years:.0f}")
```

At 6.68 percent a year India reaches half the U.S. level after **24.7 years**, around 2047; at its 2000–2022 pace of
4.83 percent it takes **36.7 years**, until about 2059. The Rule-of-70 view gives the same picture: at a growth gap of
$6.68 - 1.11 = 5.57$ points the gap halves every $70/5.57 = 12.6$ years, and it must halve
$\log_2 3.77 = 1.9$ times. Faster growth by 1.85 points a year brings the date forward by 12 years.

</details>

### Data-based problems

**Problem 4 (Basic): The Great Divergence in one number.** The file `maddison_world.csv` holds GDP per person
(2022 dollars) for 169 countries from the
[Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023).
Find the richest and the poorest country in 1870 and in 2022, and the ratio of their GDP per person. How many
countries have an estimate in each year, and how does that affect the comparison?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`maddison[maddison.year == 1870]` keeps one year. `.idxmax()` gives the row label of the largest value, and
`.loc[...]` then picks that row. `len(...)` counts the countries. To compare like with like, you can keep in 2022
only the countries that also appear in 1870.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

For each year, keep its rows, find the rows of the largest and the smallest GDP per person, and divide. Then repeat
2022 with the 1870 countries only.

```python
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
for year in [1870, 2022]:
    one_year = maddison[maddison.year == year]
    richest = one_year.loc[one_year.gdppc.idxmax()]
    poorest = one_year.loc[one_year.gdppc.idxmin()]
    print(f"{year}: {len(one_year)} countries; {richest.country} {richest.gdppc:,} / "
          f"{poorest.country} {poorest.gdppc:,} = {richest.gdppc / poorest.gdppc:.1f}")
in_1870 = maddison[maddison.year == 1870].country
same = maddison[(maddison.year == 2022) & maddison.country.isin(in_1870)]
print(f"2022, the same {len(same)} countries: {same.gdppc.max() / same.gdppc.min():.1f}")
```

In 1870 the richest country, the United Kingdom (7,520 dollars), was **9.1 times** as rich as the poorest, Nepal
(827 dollars). In 2022 Qatar (192,456 dollars) was **250 times** as rich as the Central African Republic (769 dollars).
But only 70 countries have an estimate for 1870, against 169 in 2022: in Sub-Saharan Africa only Liberia and South
Africa have one, and Qatar is an oil exporter with fewer than 3 million people. Among the same 70 countries, the ratio in 2022 is **108.9** (Norway against
Liberia). Either way, the gap between the richest and the poorest grew more than tenfold: that is the Great
Divergence.

</details>

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Booms, busts and the average growth rate.** The file `fig3-2.csv` holds U.S. GDP per
person (2022 dollars) from 1870 to 2025: from 1929 it comes from the
[Bureau of Economic Analysis, real GDP (`GDPCA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPCA) and the BEA's
population, and before 1929 from the
[Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023).

(a) Compute the growth rate of every year. Which five years saw the largest falls? Match them with the U.S.
recessions dated by the [NBER](https://www.nber.org/research/data/us-business-cycle-expansions-and-contractions).

(b) For 1870–2025, 1870–1949 and 1950–2025, compare the plain average of the yearly growth rates with the average
annual growth rate of equation (6).

(c) In which period is the gap between the two averages larger? Compare the standard deviations of the yearly growth
rates, and explain.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

`.pct_change()` gives the growth rate from each year to the next, and `.sort_values().head(5)` lists the five
smallest. For (c), recall step 5 of the derivation of equation (6): a rise of 10 percent followed by a fall of
10 percent.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Compute the yearly growth rates once, list the smallest, and then, for each period, compare their mean with
`growth_rate` applied to the first and the last year.

```python
us_gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-2.csv").set_index("year").gdppc
yearly = us_gdp.pct_change().dropna()                 # the growth rate of each year, from 1871
print((100 * yearly.sort_values().head(5)).round(1))
for first, last in [(1870, 2025), (1870, 1949), (1950, 2025)]:
    rates = yearly.loc[first + 1:last]
    plain = 100 * rates.mean()
    eq6 = 100 * growth_rate(us_gdp[first], us_gdp[last], last - first)
    print(f"{first}-{last}: plain average {plain:.2f}%, equation (6) {eq6:.2f}%, "
          f"standard deviation {100 * rates.std():.1f}%")
```

**(a)** The five largest falls are 1932 (−13.5 percent), 1946 (−12.5), 1914 (−10.0), 1908 (−9.8) and 1930 (−9.5).
1930 and 1932 fall in the NBER's contraction of August 1929 to March 1933: the Great Depression. 1908 and 1914 fall in
the contractions of May 1907 to June 1908 and January 1913 to December 1914 (before 1929 these are estimates). 1946 is
the first year after World War II, when war production was cut back.

**(b)** From 1870 to 2025 the plain average is 1.99 percent and equation (6) gives 1.88 percent. For 1870–1949 the two
are 1.92 and 1.72 percent; for 1950–2025, 1.99 and 1.97 percent.

**(c)** The gap is about 0.2 points before 1950 and only 0.02 points after. The standard deviation of the yearly growth
rates was 6.3 percent before 1950 and 2.2 percent after: the early economy swung far more. A fall hurts more than an
equal rise helps ($1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99$), so the plain average overstates growth, and more so the bigger the swings.
A handy rule is that the gap is about half the variance: $0.063^2/2 = 0.0020$, or 0.2 points. Use equation (6) for
growth over a period.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Intermediate): Argentina's century of relative decline.** Alan Taylor describes Argentina's economic
history as one of the most dramatic cases of divergence in modern times
([Taylor 2014, NBER Working Paper 19924](https://www.nber.org/papers/w19924)). Compare it in `maddison_world.csv`
with two other countries rich in land and settled by immigrants, Australia and Canada.

(a) Compute the GDP per person of Argentina, Australia and Canada relative to the United States in 1913 and in 2022.

(b) Compute the average annual growth rate of the four countries from 1913 to 2022.

(c) How rich would Argentina have been in 2022 if it had grown as fast as Australia since 1913? Compare this with its
actual level.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Turn the four countries into a wide table, one column per country, with `.pivot(index="year", columns="country",
values="gdppc")`, as in the Key numbers of Fig. 6. Then `growth_rate` gives (b), and `constant_growth` gives (c).

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Make the wide table, divide each year's row by the U.S. value, then apply equation (6) and equation (2).

```python
maddison = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
four_names = ["Argentina", "Australia", "Canada", "United States"]
four = maddison[maddison.country.isin(four_names)].pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
for year in [1913, 2022]:
    print(year, (four.loc[year] / four.loc[year, "United States"]).round(2).to_dict())
for name in four_names:
    print(f"{name}: {growth_rate(four.loc[1913, name], four.loc[2022, name], 109):.2%} a year")
g_aus = growth_rate(four.loc[1913, "Australia"], four.loc[2022, "Australia"], 109)
what_if = constant_growth(four.loc[1913, "Argentina"], g_aus, 109)
print(f"Argentina at Australia's rate: {what_if:,.0f} dollars, {what_if / four.loc[2022, 'Argentina']:.1f} times its actual level")
```

**(a)** In 1913 Argentina had 60 percent of U.S. GDP per person, Canada 70 percent and Australia 81 percent. In 2022
Argentina had 31 percent, while Canada had risen to 78 percent and Australia to 89 percent.

**(b)** From 1913 to 2022, GDP per person grew 1.02 percent a year in Argentina, 1.71 percent in Australia,
1.72 percent in Canada and 1.62 percent in the United States.

**(c)** At Australia's 1.71 percent, Argentina's 7,808 dollars of 1913 would have become about 49,400 dollars in 2022,
**2.1 times** its actual 23,600 dollars. A gap of 0.7 points a year looks small, but by the ratio rule it makes
Argentina's income relative to Australia's fall about 0.7 percent a year, which halves it in about $70/0.7 = 100$
years. That is what happened: Argentina had 74 percent of Australia's GDP per person in 1913 and 35 percent in 2022.

</details>

**Problem 7 (Challenge): A fairer test of catch-up.** Fig. 7 plots each country's growth against its income in
*2023*, and the chapter warns that its upward tilt is partly built in. Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian (2021) find that
poorer countries have been catching up with richer ones, slowly, since the mid-1990s
([Journal of Development Economics, doi:10.1016/j.jdeveco.2021.102687](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2021.102687)).
Check this with `pwt_income.csv` from the [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/), for
the 110 countries of Fig. 7 (those with `in_sample` true, without Venezuela).

(a) Compute each country's average annual growth rate of GDP per person from 1960 to 2023, and from 2000 to 2023.

(b) For each period, compute the correlation of growth with the log of GDP per person relative to the United States
in the *starting* year, and with the log of relative GDP per person in 2023.

(c) What do the four correlations say about convergence? How many countries grew faster than the United States in
each period?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Build one table per starting year with `merge`, as the code of Fig. 7 does, and add a column with
`np.log(...)` of relative income. `table.growth.corr(table.log_start)` gives a correlation. For (c), ask why a
country that grew fast *must* end up rich, whatever its start.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

For each starting year, merge the start-year and 2023 values, compute growth with equation (6), divide by the U.S.
value of the same year, take logs and correlate.

```python
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_income.csv")
panel = panel[panel.in_sample & (panel.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)")]
last_year = panel[panel.year == 2023][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]
for start_year in [1960, 2000]:
    pair = panel[panel.year == start_year][["iso3", "country", "gdp_pc"]].merge(last_year, on="iso3",
                                                                                suffixes=("_start", "_2023"))
    pair["growth"] = 100 * growth_rate(pair.gdp_pc_start, pair.gdp_pc_2023, 2023 - start_year)
    usa_row = pair[pair.country == "United States"].iloc[0]
    pair["log_start"] = np.log(pair.gdp_pc_start / usa_row.gdp_pc_start)
    pair["log_2023"] = np.log(pair.gdp_pc_2023 / usa_row.gdp_pc_2023)
    print(f"{start_year}-2023, {len(pair)} countries: correlation with the start level "
          f"{pair.growth.corr(pair.log_start):.2f}, with the 2023 level {pair.growth.corr(pair.log_2023):.2f}; "
          f"{(pair.growth > usa_row.growth).sum()} grew faster than the U.S. ({usa_row.growth:.2f}%)")
```

**(a)–(b)** For 1960–2023 the correlation of growth with the starting level is −0.05, and with the 2023 level +0.66.
For 2000–2023 it is −0.34 with the starting level and −0.05 with the 2023 level.

**(c)** The +0.66 of Fig. 7's view is mostly built in: a country that grew fast became rich by 2023, whatever its
start. Against the *starting* level, 1960–2023 shows almost no relation: on average, poor countries in 1960 did not
grow faster than rich ones, so there was no catch-up across the world as a whole. Since 2000 the correlation is
negative, −0.34: poorer countries grew faster on average, as Patel, Sandefur and Subramanian find. It is still weak,
so catch-up is slow and many poor countries lag. From 1960, 64 of the 110 countries grew faster than the United States
(2.03 percent a year); from 2000, 85 did (the U.S. grew 1.32 percent a year).

</details>

### Modeling problems

**Problem 8 (Basic): Will the world's population double again?** The United Nations reports that the world
population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022, twelve years after it passed 7 billion. It expects 9 billion in
about 15 years, around 2037, and a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s
([United Nations, Global Issues: Population](https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/population)). Food and energy planners
want to know how soon the world will need twice as much as today. The widget is the doubling chart of Fig. 4 with a
finer slider for the growth rate. It starts at 6 billion, but the doubling time does not depend on the starting level.

(a) What was the average annual growth rate of the world population from 7 to 8 billion? Set the slider close to it:
how many years would a doubling take at that rate?

(b) Do the same for the UN's path from 8 to 9 billion.

(c) What average growth rate takes the world from 8 billion in 2022 to 10.3 billion around 2085? Why can a constant
growth rate never produce a peak? What population in 2085 would a planner predict by extending the growth rate of (a)?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Use equation (6) with the two population levels and the number of years between them. The chart's title then gives
the exact doubling time, equation (4), and the Rule of 70. For (c), equation (1) says how much a population growing at
a constant $\bar{n}$ adds in a year.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def world_doubling(n=0.015):
    """Fig. 3.4 with a finer slider: the doubling time of equation (4) for the growth rate n."""
    fig = population_two_scales(n)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"n = {100 * n:.2f}%: doubles every {doubling_time(n):.1f} years "
                            f"(Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})")
    return fig


interact(world_doubling,
         n=FloatSlider(value=0.015, min=0.003, max=0.025, step=0.0005, description="growth rate n", style=WIDE,
                       readout_format=".4f"));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 4 above, adapted from Fig. 3.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```python
paths = [("7 to 8 billion", 7, 8, 12), ("8 to 9 billion", 8, 9, 15), ("8 to 10.3 billion", 8, 10.3, 63)]
for name, low, high, years in paths:
    n_path = growth_rate(low, high, years)
    print(f"{name}: n = {100 * n_path:.2f}% a year, doubling time {doubling_time(n_path):.1f} years "
          f"(Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n_path):.1f})")
print(f"8 billion at the 7-to-8 rate for 63 years: {constant_growth(8, growth_rate(7, 8, 12), 63):.1f} billion")
```

**(a)** Equation (6) gives $\bar{n} = (8/7)^{1/12} - 1 = 0.0112$, or **1.12 percent a year**. On the slider, 1.10 percent
gives a doubling time of 63.4 years and 1.15 percent gives 60.6 years. The exact doubling time is
$\ln 2/\ln(1+\bar{n}) = 12\ln 2/\ln(8/7) = 62.3$ years (Rule of 70: 62.6).

**(b)** From 8 to 9 billion in 15 years, $\bar{n} = (9/8)^{1/15} - 1 = 0.0079$, or **0.79 percent a year**. The slider at
0.80 percent shows 87.0 years; the exact doubling time is $15\ln 2/\ln(9/8) = 88.3$ years (Rule of 70: 88.8).

**(c)** From 8 to 10.3 billion in 63 years, $\bar{n} = (10.3/8)^{1/63} - 1 = 0.0040$, only **0.40 percent a year**, with a
doubling time of 172.8 years. But a constant growth rate can never produce a peak. By equation (1), a population
growing at a constant $\bar{n} > 0$ adds $\bar{n}L_t$ people every year, a positive amount that grows with $L_t$, so the
population rises forever. A peak needs a growth rate that falls to zero and then turns negative, which is what the UN
expects as birth rates keep falling. A planner who extended the 1.12 percent of 2010–2022 would predict
**16.1 billion** people in 2085, almost 6 billion more than the UN's peak. On the UN's projections, the world
population will not double again from 8 billion, so plans built on a constant growth rate would greatly overstate
future needs.

</details>

**Problem 9 (Intermediate): Fewer births, faster growth?** In 2022 a woman in Niger had about 6.1 children on
average, against 2.2 in Bangladesh, where the fertility rate has fallen from 6.8 in 1970
([World Bank, World Development Indicators, Fertility rate, total (`SP.DYN.TFRT.IN`)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.TFRT.IN?locations=BD-NE)).
The widget is the chart of Fig. 9 for five countries of Africa and South Asia.

(a) Set the period to 1990–2022. Read the growth rates of total GDP, GDP per person and population in Niger and in
Bangladesh. At these rates, how many years does GDP per person take to double in each country?

(b) A policy adviser argues: "If Niger's population grew as slowly as Bangladesh's, while its GDP kept growing at the
same rate, its GDP per person would double within a generation." Use the ratio rule to check the claim.

(c) Population growth is also growth of the labor force. Use equation (10), keeping productivity growth $g_A$ and
capital growth $g_K$ unchanged, to show why the adviser is too optimistic. How fast would Niger's GDP per person then
grow, and how long would it take to double?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(b) Keep $g_Y$ fixed in $g_y = g_Y - g_L$. (c) Per person, equation (10) becomes $g_y = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}(g_K - g_L)$,
as the Model overview shows. How much does $g_y$ change when $g_L$ falls by one point?

</details>

         period=IntRangeSlider(value=(1990, 2022), min=1950, max=2022, step=1, description="period", style=WIDE),

**Source.** The chart of Fig. 9 above, with data from the [Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)
(Bolt and van Zanden 2024), inspired by Fig. 3.9 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```python
for country_name in ["Niger", "Bangladesh"]:
    print(growth_rules_chart((1990, 2022), country_name).layout.title.text)
gY, gL_niger, gL_bangladesh, gy_niger = 0.0410, 0.0364, 0.0141, 0.0045
gy_rule = gY - gL_bangladesh                            # (b): ratio rule, GDP growth unchanged
gy_eq10 = gy_niger + (gL_niger - gL_bangladesh) / 3     # (c): equation (10), g_A and g_K unchanged
for name, rate in [("actual", gy_niger), ("(b) ratio rule", gy_rule), ("(c) equation (10)", gy_eq10)]:
    print(f"{name}: GDP per person grows {100 * rate:.2f}% a year and doubles in {doubling_time(rate):.0f} years")
```

**(a)** From 1990 to 2022, Niger's GDP grew 4.10 percent a year, but its population grew 3.64 percent, so GDP per
person grew only 0.45 percent: it doubles in about **154 years**. Bangladesh's GDP grew 6.57 percent and its
population 1.41 percent, so GDP per person grew 5.09 percent and doubles in about **14 years**.

**(b)** With $g_Y = 4.10$ and $g_L = 1.41$ percent, the ratio rule gives $g_y = 4.10 - 1.41 = 2.69$ percent, which
doubles GDP per person in about **26 years**. On this arithmetic the adviser is right.

**(c)** But GDP growth would not stay the same. Population growth falls by $\Delta = 3.64 - 1.41 = 2.23$ points, so by
equation (10) labor adds $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 2.23 = 1.49$ points less to GDP growth. Per person,
$g_y = g_A + \tfrac{1}{3}(g_K - g_L)$ rises by only $\Delta/3 = 0.74$ points, to $0.45 + 0.74 = 1.19$ percent a year:
the same capital is spread over fewer people, but fewer workers also produce less. GDP per person then doubles in
about **58 years**, not 26. Slower population growth helps, but only a third as much as the adviser thinks. By the same
equation, Bangladesh's lower population growth explains only a small part of its 4.64-point lead over Niger in growth
per person; the rest must come from faster growth of productivity and of capital per person, the subject of
Chapters 4 to 6.

</details>

**Problem 10 (Challenge): Can poverty fall to 3 percent by 2030?** In 2013 the World Bank and the IMF's Development
Committee endorsed the goal of cutting the share of the world's people in extreme poverty to 3 percent by 2030
([IMF, Transcript of the Development Committee press briefing, 20 April 2013](https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2015/09/28/04/54/tr042013a)).
The World Bank now counts people living on less than \$3 a day as extremely poor
([World Bank, Poverty overview](https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/poverty/overview)). Fig. 8 uses a simpler
measure: the share of people who live in countries whose GDP per person is below 5 percent of the 2019 U.S. level,
about 3,400 dollars a year at 2021 prices.

(a) Use the widget to read the share of people below the line in 1990, 2010, 2019 and 2023.

(b) A falling share has a negative growth rate. Compute its average annual growth rate from 1990 to 2019 with
equation (6). Derive a halving rule like the Rule of 70: about how many years does the share take to halve at that
pace? At the 1990–2019 pace, in what year would the share reach 3 percent?

(c) Repeat (b) for 2010–2023. Which projection do you trust more, and why? Hover over the steps of the chart: what
made the share fall so fast before 2010, and who is left below the line?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(b) Put $y_t = y_0/2$ into equation (2) and follow the steps that led to equation (4). For the 3 percent date, use
$t = \ln m/\ln(1+\bar{g})$ with $m = 0.03$ divided by the latest share. (c) `cumulative_shares(2023)` lists the
countries and their incomes; compare the shares of 2015 and 2019 too.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(population_distribution,
         year=Dropdown(options=[1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2023], value=1990, description="year", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** The chart of Fig. 8 above, with data from the [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/)
(Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015), inspired by Fig. 3.8 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

```python
poor_share = {}
for year in [1990, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2023]:
    shares_year = cumulative_shares(year)
    below = shares_year[shares_year.y_rel_us_2019 < 0.05]
    poor_share[year] = below.pop_millions.sum() / shares_year.pop_millions.sum()
    print(f"{year}: {poor_share[year]:.1%} of people below the line")
for first, last in [(1990, 2019), (2010, 2023)]:
    g_share = growth_rate(poor_share[first], poor_share[last], last - first)
    to_3 = np.log(0.03 / poor_share[last]) / np.log(1 + g_share)
    print(f"{first}-{last}: {100 * g_share:.2f}% a year, halves in {np.log(0.5) / np.log(1 + g_share):.1f} years, "
          f"3% in {last + to_3:.0f}, {constant_growth(poor_share[last], g_share, 2030 - last):.1%} in 2030")
print(below.sort_values("pop_millions").tail(5)[["country", "pop_millions", "y_rel_us_2019"]])
```

**(a)** The chart's titles show about 60 percent in 1990, 11 percent in 2010, 9 percent in 2019 and 8 percent in 2023
(the code gives 59.7, 11.3, 8.5 and 7.8 percent).

**(b)** Equation (6) gives $\bar{g} = (0.0854/0.5973)^{1/29} - 1 = -0.0649$: the share fell **6.49 percent a year**, a
percentage of itself, not percentage points. For the halving time, $(1+\bar{g})^t = 1/2$ gives

$$t_{\text{half}} = \frac{\ln(1/2)}{\ln(1+\bar{g})} = \frac{-\ln 2}{\ln(1+\bar{g})} \approx \frac{0.693}{|\bar{g}|} \approx \frac{70}{|g|},$$

with $g$ in percent, the Rule of 70 for a decline. At 6.49 percent it gives $70/6.49 = 10.8$ years; the exact value is
**10.3 years**. (For a decline the rule overstates the time a little, because $\ln(1+\bar{g})$ is more negative than
$\bar{g}$.) The share then reaches 3 percent $\ln(0.03/0.0854)/\ln(0.9351) = 15.6$ years after 2019, in **2035**; in
2030 it would still be 4.1 percent.

**(c)** From 2010 to 2023 the share fell only **2.78 percent a year**: it halves every 24.5 years, reaches 3 percent
only in **2057**, and would be 6.4 percent in 2030. The second projection is the better guide, and it says that on this
measure the 3 percent goal will be missed. A constant rate of decline fits these data badly, because the share falls in
steps: when a very populous country crosses the line, its whole population leaves the poor group at once. Hovering
shows China crossing the line in the 1990s and India in the 2000s (in these data, in 1996 and 2006), which took the share
from 60 percent in 1990 to 11 percent in 2010. That cannot happen again. The largest countries still below the line in
2023 are Ethiopia (129 million people), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (106 million), Uganda, Mozambique and
Madagascar. Their populations grow fast, which raises their share of the world's people: the share even rose from
8.2 percent in 2015 to 8.5 percent in 2019. Reaching the goal requires growth in these poorest, fast-growing countries.

</details>
